My Review:
Dead Beat!!!!

Bardugo has already proven she can blend dread, dark humor, and mythology better than Jamba Juice blends smoothies, so my faith is absolute. I’m clearing my schedule, my brain, and possibly my moral compass for this one.

At this point I’m experiencing full-body withdrawals for the Yale weirdness, the occult academia, and the “we survived hell together but still can’t have a normal conversation” tension that only Alex and Darlington can deliver.

My wishlist is simple:
• smart, tense, character-driven chaos
• beautifully unhinged magical academia
• Alex and Darlington finally confronting… whatever it is they’re avoiding

Title: Ice
Author: Anna Kavan
My Review:
I understand why it’s a cult classic. I’m still not sure I understand why people love it.

It’s surreal, apocalyptic, dreamlike, and genuinely unlike anything else I’ve read. But I spent most of the book wondering: what is happening, who are these people, and why should I care?

By the end, I understood what Kavan was doing. The dream logic, the obsession, the symbolism, the nightmare atmosphere. I just found the actual reading experience… kind of average.

Interesting? Absolutely. A favorite? Not even remotely.

2.75/5 ⭐️ feels about right.

What am I missing?

Title: 84, Charing Cross Road
Author: Helene Hanff
My Review:
This is the book equivalent of a perfect afternoon: over quickly, pleasant throughout, and not especially demanding of you. Whether that's a compliment depends entirely on what you came for.

This is a real epistolary memoir, a collection of letters exchanged over twenty years between Hanff, a broke New York writer with expensive literary tastes, and Frank, the chief buyer at Marks & Co., an antiquarian bookshop.

Hanff orders obscure classics she can't find stateside. Frank fulfills them with dry efficiency. Over time, something warmer develops, expanding to include the shop staff, Frank's family, and a neighbor or two. It's charming, occasionally funny, and in the final pages, genuinely sad.

The pleasure here is almost entirely tonal. Hanff's voice is brash, funny, and completely her own, and the contrast between her breezy American informality and Frank's measured British reserve makes their correspondence a masterclass in what letters can do that prose can't.

But the ceiling is real. Frank stays somewhat opaque throughout, and the relationship never quite achieves the depth the book seems to claim for it.

This is a book for readers who loves books about books, those who have a soft spot for epistolary form, or those who want something warm and short that goes down easy. If that's you, it will deliver. If you want to be changed by what you read, look elsewhere.

Title: A Guardian and a Thief
Author: Megha Majumdar
My Review:
I almost passed on this one. I wasn't sure I had the bandwidth for another near-future dystopia with a message. But I'm really glad I gave it a shot.

Throughout the book I found many lines that made me smile, and others that blew me away, like this one:

"The depth of night always felt adjacent to real life, a fourth dimension of the world that allowed the honesty and courage that daylight forbade."

This is a dual narrative set over the course of a single week in a near-future Kolkata collapsing under famine and climate catastrophe. Ma's family has their passports stolen days before they are able to emigrate to Michigan. The teenager named Boomba who took them is desperate in ways Ma can't fully see from her vantage point.

I was pleasantly surprised at how charming the voice of the book is. Majumdar captures the internal lives of both characters precisely, without overwriting. Both Ma and Boomba are operating from the same ferocious love for their families, and the novel's central tension is that neither of them is wrong, exactly.

The architecture of the novel is precise — every detail doubles as social commentary: the visas, the shelter, the billionaire benefactor, the food Ma skims for her own family.

Majumdar occasionally tells you what she's already shown you, but her detail work is strong enough to overlook it.

A two-year-old asking for "flowerflower" because she's just discovered cauliflower. An old man who doesn't want to leave Kolkata but won't say so because his love for his daughter runs deeper than his grief. These are the details that make a short novel feel full, and make it a National Book Award finalist that actually deserves the distinction.

Title: Sisters in Yellow
Author: Mieko Kawakami
My Review:
Thank you to Knopf and NetGalley for providing an e-ARC in exchange for my honest review. All thoughts and opinions are my own.

The marketing for Sisters in Yellow uses phrases like “pacy,” “thrilling,” and even “Japanese Breaking Bad.” Luckily, I didn't pay attention to that and go in with any false expectations, because this book ended up reading more like a slow-burn character study than a thriller.

A big plus was that I found Kawakami's exploration of loneliness and survival to be focused. The novel successfully shows how a fixation on financial security can become a kind of emotional protection that also pushes others away. I think the book is also an effective commentary on class, poverty, and the limited choices available to women living on the margins of Japanese society.

More positives: Kawakami builds the world through small, lived-in details, and the voice fits the material well. While Hana isn’t easy to sympathize with, her behavior feels believable. The supporting cast also keeps things interesting by adding tension and uncertainty throughout. Overall, the emotional impact of the novel leans more toward sadness and unease than big drama, and that resonated with me.

The main issue for me was the pacing, mostly due to Hana’s anxieties becoming repetitive and the long monologues and stretches of exposition (especially about the mechanics of card fraud).

In the second half, some narrative threads meander instead of building momentum, and the ending feels abrupt compared to the slow buildup. The present-day framing device ends up feeling underdeveloped.

Could the novel have been shorter? Probably. Was the length unbearable? No. I think the patience will pay off for most readers who make it to the end, even though the book could have been more tightly edited.

Overall, I enjoyed Sisters in Yellow enough that I’d recommend it to readers who enjoy stories about loneliness, survival, and belonging.

My rating: 3.75/5 Stars.

Title: Death in Venice
Author: Thomas Mann
My Review:
Have you ever finished a book feeling certain it was important without being entirely sure you enjoyed it? That was Death in Venice for me.

Thomas Mann's 1912 classic follows Gustav, an aging German writer who travels to Venice and becomes consumed by an obsession with a beautiful Polish boy he never speaks to. That's the whole plot. What Mann does with it is layer symbolism, Greek philosophy, and psychological dread, all while an epidemic quietly closes in around the edges.

The prose is meticulous, ornate, and rewards close reading, but it can also feel suffocating. Everything means something. Every stranger the protagonist encounters is a mythological signpost. It's brilliantly crafted, but its density keeps you at arm's length.

I respect this more than I was moved by it. For me, it's a masterwork of atmosphere and ideas that left me admiring Mann's control while wishing he'd let me feel a little more and think a little less.

3.25/5 Stars.

Title: One Aladdin Two Lamps
Author: Jeanette Winterson
My Review:
Jeanette Winterson doesn't write books so much as she builds kaleidoscopes and dares you to look through them.

One Aladdin Two Lamps takes One Thousand and One Nights as its launchpad and then spirals outward into memoir, literary criticism, philosophy, and political commentary, all held together by Winterson's fierce argument that storytelling is how we survive. She retells Shahrazad's tales, threads in her own upbringing as a queer girl in a fundamentalist household, name-drops everyone from Shakespeare to Taylor Swift, and somehow makes it all feel like a single conversation rather than a syllabus.

When it works, it's thrilling. Winterson's prose has a clarity and directness that cuts through the sheer density of what she's attempting. But the book occasionally buckles under its own ambition. Some passages tip from passionate into preachy, and the late-stage detour into AI optimism feels oddly disconnected from the rest.

3.5/5 Stars. A dazzling, uneven love letter to the power of stories.

Title: Paradise Logic
Author: Sophie  Kemp
My Review:
Paradise Logic is 8% talking snakes, 13% excerpts from a fictional magazine called Girlfriend Weekly, 19% hallucinatory clinical trials, 15% sex scenes that will make you put the book down and stare at the ceiling, and 100% prose that reads like it was written by someone channeling Miranda July after three energy drinks and a Tumblr binge.

My reading experience felt like being trapped inside someone's unhinged group chat while they're having an existential crisis, and somehow being unable to stop scrolling.

The story follows Reality Kahn, a 23-year-old Oberlin grad living in Gowanus, Brooklyn, who goes on a surreal, fragmented, and frequently obscene odyssey to fulfill her life's purpose: finding a boyfriend and becoming the greatest girlfriend of all time.

Kemp's voice is the whole show here. Reality narrates her world with a mix of alien detachment and devastating sincerity, describing everything from sex to Coca-Cola with the same wide-eyed, off-kilter cadence. It's equally hilarious and cringey.

But make no mistake, Paradise Logic is a lot. A LOT. It knows it's a lot. Kemp knows exactly what she's doing tonally, switching between absurdist comedy and genuine heartbreak without warning, and the whiplash is part of the point. Underneath all the chaos, she sustains a sharp, sad argument about what it means to desire men in a world that punishes you for it.

The electricity of that voice will keep most readers going, at least those who aren't immediately put off. Still, I found that the narrative underneath it struggles to hold its own weight. The surreal detours pile up, the bit starts to wear thin in the back half, and by the end I wasn't sure the novel had earned its emotional crescendo so much as arrived at one. Whether the book works for you will depend entirely on how long you can ride a vibe before you start wanting a story. For me, it was about three-quarters of the way.

That said, I'm genuinely glad this book exists. It's doing something fearless, and any comparisons to Miranda July or Mona Awad feel right without fully capturing what Paradise Logic offers. I left wanting more from the bones of this one even as I admired it. Read it if you're in the mood to feel unsettled and entertained in equal measure. Skip it if you need narrative to be the thing pulling you forward.

3/5 Stars.

Title: Cat’s Cradle
Author: Kurt Vonnegut Jr.
My Review:
Only Vonnegut could write a book about the end of the world that reads like a comedian's set at a funeral, and somehow leave you feeling more alive by the last page.

Cat's Cradle follows a writer named John who is researching Dr. Hoenikker, one of the fictional fathers of the atomic bomb. This project quickly spirals into something far stranger, pulling John through Hoenikker's three dysfunctional children, a religion that admits everything it teaches is a lie, and a discovery that makes the atomic bomb look like a warm-up act.

The pacing in Cat's cradle is relentless, but don't think that short sentences and absurdly brief chapters (127 of them in under 300 pages) equals lack of depth. The humor here is doing serious work: a deadpan narrator reports catastrophe with the same energy he'd use to order breakfast, and underneath every joke is a quiet horror about what happens when brilliant people build terrible things and shrug at the consequences.

Readers will notice that Vonnegut can't be bothered to slow down for scenery when there's a point to be made, and this might make it feel like impatience is the book's main limitation. Characters appear, reveal something essential about human nature in a paragraph, and get swept along. They function as satirical sketches more than fully realized people. If you need to feel deeply connected to the characters in a story, this one may leave you cold. You may find the many threads in the novel lack cohesion. But the book is widely loved for its inventiveness, its biting commentary on science and religion, and the way it manages to be one of the bleakest and most oddly tender things Vonnegut ever wrote.

I settled on 3.75/5 stars because Vonnegut's ideas in Cat's Cradle are brilliant, the voice is iconic, and I'll be turning over lines like "beware of the man who works hard to learn something, learns it, and finds himself no wiser than before" for a long time. I just wanted a little more room to care about these people before the book's ending. Cat's Cradle will likely hit the spot if you pick this up when you want something sharp, strange, and wickedly smart that you can devour in an afternoon or two.

Title: The Correspondent
Author: Virginia      Evans
My Review:
"You get the one life. It's awfully unfair, isn't it?"

If you've ever felt the weight that life is too short and too long all at once, Virginia Evans has written a book that will sit with you for a very long time.

The Correspondent is the story of Sybil, a retired 73-year-old who has built her life around letters. Every morning she writes. She sends letters to her brother, her best friend, to authors (Joan Didion, Larry McMurtry, Ann Patchett!) to tell them what she thinks of their latest books, and to one person to whom she writes often but never sends the letter. Through her correspondences, we piece together a life shaped by love, grief, and regret. When letters from someone in Sybil's past force her to confront the loss of her young son Gilbert, she begins to realize that the unsent letter she's been composing for years may finally need to be read.

The novel is told entirely in letters and the occasional email. There is no narrator, no traditional scenes, no dialogue, and yet Evans manages to avoid gimmick territory entirely. That's largely because of Sybil herself, who is sharp-tongued, opinionated, sometimes maddeningly stubborn, and underneath it all, deeply wounded. By the end you don't feel like you've read a novel. You feel like you've gone through someone's private mail and come out knowing them better than most people in their life do.

You spend the whole book playing detective, assembling Sybil's story from scattered puzzle pieces, and that gradual reveal is one of the book's greatest pleasures. Her character development is equally rewarding. She begins as someone who seems fully formed and prickly, but letter by letter, Evans peels back those layers to reveal the grief and loneliness she's been papering over with eloquence and propriety.

Fair warning: the epistolary format can feel disjointed if you prefer linear, plot-driven storytelling. But this book rewards patience. In the landscape of modern fiction, it occupies a lovely, slightly old-fashioned space, and it's all the better for it.

I gave this 5/5 stars because it is highly entertaining and enjoyable character-driven fiction that convinced me that even a quiet story about an ordinary woman can be every bit as profound as an epic. If you're in the mood to slow down or you need to be reminded that it's never too late to say the thing you've been meaning to say, you should read it!

Title: The Remains of the Day
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
Some novels devastate you loudly. The Remains of the Day devastates you through silence.

The book follows Stevens, an English butler taking a motoring trip in the 1950s while reflecting on his decades of service to Lord Darlington and his relationship with Miss Kenton. What unfolds is not dramatic in a conventional sense, but rather a slow realization that a life built entirely around duty can leave very little room for the self.

This is one of Ishiguro’s defining novels, and you can see why it is so often praised. Stevens tells his story in a formal, careful voice, always emphasizing dignity and loyalty. What makes the book powerful is what he avoids saying. The emotional weight lives between the lines. As readers, we slowly piece together what Stevens cannot fully face about his employer, his choices, and his own heart.

The themes of duty, complicity, repression, and class are handled with remarkable control. The pacing is quiet and measured, which is why some readers consider it a masterpiece while others find it slow or emotionally distant. Both reactions make sense. If you prefer plot-heavy stories or highly expressive characters, this might feel restrained. If you enjoy subtle character studies, it is deeply rewarding.

For me, it is a 3.5/5 stars-- there's nothing I actively dislike about the novel, but when it comes down to it, I admire it more than I love it. Even so, it remains a carefully crafted story with a quietly heartbreaking ending, and a great fit for readers who appreciate thoughtful, layered stories where the real drama happens beneath the surface.

Title: Wild Dark Shore
Author: Charlotte McConaghy
My Review:
What stayed with me most about Wild Dark Shore was not the plot, but how McConaghy slowly builds its emotional architecture.

The story unfolds in a setting that shapes the characters as much as they shape it, with isolation, memory, and connection at its center. Rather than relying on constant twists, the novel moves, at times deliberately slowly, through subtle relationship changes.

McConaghy expertly uses a tone that is controlled and sometimes lyrical, along with restrained character development, to create a gradual build that has a strong overall effect. Even in emotionally charged moments, the prose remains grounded and precise.

One line captures an idea that echoes throughout the book:
“But here is the nature of life. That we must love things with our whole selves, knowing they will die.”

Despite its literary style, the novel has broad appeal because its themes are universal, including love, loss, and isolation. It resonates beyond genre boundaries because it is emotionally accessible and thoughtfully written.

I rate Wild Dark Shore 4/5 stars because it was a satisfying read with just a few nitpicks that kept it from being perfect for me. Its strengths far outweigh its limitations. It is no surprise this novel won the Book of the Month 2025 Lolly Award and was also a Goodreads Nominee for Readers’ Favorite Fiction (2025).

Title: The Idiot
Author: Elif Batuman
My Review:
Is the rock on the cover meant to suggest, “this is your brain on The Idiot”? Because I think I felt my brain slowly petrify while I read this book.

The Idiot follows Selin as she drifts through her first year of college. She befriends a small circle of eccentric classmates, enrolls in a Russian class that quietly shapes her inner life, and becomes fixated on a strange, elliptical email correspondence with an older Hungarian math student. Not much “happens” in a traditional plot sense, but the novel traces Selin’s attempts to interpret language, relationships, and herself.

I wanted to love this book. On paper, the awkward intellectual coming-of-age and deadpan humor should have worked. Yet, the narrators inability to turn experience into meaning became my own.

To her credit, Batuman fully commits to the bit. The voice is precise, alien, often very funny. The academic satire and early-email awkwardness are sharp and painfully accurate.

But admiration isn’t the same as enjoyment. The Ivan storyline circles without deepening, and the book’s refusal of catharsis started to feel airless rather than profound.

This is for readers who love interiority over plot, anti-climax over transformation, and the slow study of a mind thinking itself into corners. It just wasn’t for me.

Title: Concrete
Author: Thomas Bernhard
My Review:
Concrete is a funny, claustrophobic monologue about a man who cannot begin the book he believes will justify his existence.

Rudolf, a reclusive Viennese musicologist, has been “about to” write his definitive study of Mendelssohn for years. Instead of writing he rambles on and on about his domineering sister, his lung disease, the stupidity of society, the impossibility of concentration, the catastrophe of other people. The delightful irony is that the book we are reading is, in fact, the masterpiece he cannot write.

Sure, the way Bernhard weaponizes repetition here is monotonous by design and can be suffocatingly interior. But, the relentless looping morphs into comedy, and in my opinion, if you appreciate the humor of authors like Beckett, this will likely be right up your alley.

The bottom line is that you don’t read Concrete for plot, you read it for Rudolf’s voice and to inhabit a mind that is eroding itself in real time.

For me, it’s a strong 4/5. A novel about NOT writing, that’s razor-sharp, disturbingly funny, and in many moments brilliant.

Title: Whistler
Author: Ann Patchett
My Review:
I haven’t cracked the spine yet, but it is Ann Patchett, so I am expecting elegance, insight, and at least one moment that makes me marvel at how small, fleeting choices can alter a life.

Whistler promises a reunion decades in the making, love that persists in quiet ways, and a meditation on memory, bravery, and all the little moments that shape who we become. If Patchett has taught us anything in books like Bel Canto, it is that she can make a single scene, whether a glance in a museum, a whispered conversation, or a memory recalled, feel like the hinge of the universe.

I am ready to be fully swept up in Daphne and Eddie’s story. Consider this 5/5 stars in advance because I trust Patchett will deliver.

Title: Culpability
Author: Bruce Holsinger
My Review:
Family on vacation colliding with AI is a premise that could have been thrilling. Instead, Culpability flops spectacularly. The single setting makes the story feel cramped and repetitive. The tragedies that are supposed to shake the characters barely register. Their responses are shallow, perfunctory, almost comically underwhelming.

The AI elements of this story lean hard on clichés that have been done to death, and the endless twists where every character is hiding a secret feel forced to the point of absurdity. Stakes are inflated, suspense is manufactured, and I could not care less. The characters are thin sketches at best, leaving no emotional anchor as the story progresses.

A few hints at human agency and blame in a machine-dominated world almost shine, but they are too little, too late. The middle drags endlessly, the tension is fake, and the story never hits. Culpability may be passably readable, but it is also painfully unremarkable.

Title: Partita
Author: Barbara Kingsolver
My Review:
I haven’t read a single page yet, but here’s what I do know: Barbara Kingsolver is about to hit us with heartbreak, class commentary, music metaphors, and at least one character who makes you question all your life choices.

If Demon Copperhead taught me anything, it’s that Kingsolver can make you laugh, gasp, and marvel at the sheer precision of her storytelling. Partita promises all that, but with pianos, ghosts from the past, and a protagonist juggling love, ambition, and long-buried secrets.

I’m here for it. I will be fully invested in Livia Cable’s choices, cheer for her triumphs, and probably celebrate every exquisitely framed sentence.

5/5 stars in advance, because optimism.

Title: The Sorrows of Young Werther
Author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
Additional Authors: Burton Pike, R. Dillon Boylan, Elizabeth Wolff Mayer
My Review:
There’s a good reason The Sorrows of Young Werther caused a cultural phenomenon when it was published in 1774.

The novel sparked “Werther Fever.” Young readers dressed like him. Some tragically imitated him. It became one of the first true global literary sensations. Reading The Sorrows of Young Werther today feels like discovering the original blueprint for the emotionally obsessive literary protagonist.

The book unfolds through letters written by the sensitive and passionate Werther, who relocates to the countryside in search of peace, beauty, and artistic inspiration. Instead, he becomes consumed by an intense emotional attachment that grows into an existential crisis.

It’s striking how modern the book feels: the confessional voice, the emotional immediacy, the relentless self-analysis, the romantic idealization of nature, the spiraling interior monologue. Werther’s voice must have felt radically new when it first appeared, and it still feels fresh today. You can see its descendants everywhere, from Dostoevsky’s tortured narrators to Proust’s hypersensitivity, to the emotionally articulate characters of contemporary literary fiction.

Though the novel has a reputation for being relentlessly tragic, it’s often quietly funny. Goethe understands the absurdity of youthful intensity. Werther is melodramatic, impulsive, and gloriously over-poetic about everyday life. But Goethe skillfully maintains a perfect balance in the narration that signals that he clearly loves Werther, but he also sees him with gentle clarity.

The novel is a philosophical argument disguised as a love story. Werther embodies emotion as a way of life. Opposing him is the world of rationality, moderation, and social order. Watching his psychological progression from idealism to attachment, to emotional dependency, to existential crisis, is what makes this a five-star read for me. Goethe charts that progression with unsettling precision.

Every letter in the book raises the emotional temperature. The pacing mirrors Werther’s spiraling obsession. It’s a masterclass in how structure can reflect psychology.

This novel helped create:
• the Romantic hero
• the confessional narrator
• the interior emotional novel
• the idea that a character’s inner life can be the plot

It’s staggering to remember Goethe wrote this in his twenties. You can feel the young genius pouring his own emotional life into the pages.

The Sorrows of Young Werther endures because it understands the timeless concept of intoxicating beauty and the real danger of feeling too much. Nearly 250 years later, it still feels painfully, vividly relevant.

Title: Departure[s]
Author: Julian Barnes
My Review:
Reading Departure(s) feels like pulling up a chair with the Booker Prize–winning author for one last quiet conversation.

In this book, Barnes leans less on conventional storytelling and more on a blend of memoir, essay, and reflection. He meditates on happiness, love, aging, and the art of writing itself, offering readers a window into the mind of one of contemporary literature’s sharpest observers.

Barnes’ personality shines throughout. He's witty, reflective, and unflinchingly honest. While the book lacks the narrative tension or plot-driven momentum of his novels, his voice remains engaging, making the experience quietly satisfying.

For fans of Barnes, this is a rare opportunity to read his last words of wisdom and reflection. I’m giving it 3.75/5, largely for the insight and charm of his voice.

Title: Post Office
Author: Charles Bukowski
My Review:
“We’re forced into absurd lives, against which the only sane response is to wage a guerrilla operation of humour and lust and madness.”

Post Office follows Henry Chinaski, Charles Bukowski’s alter ego, as he drifts into a job at the U.S. Postal Service and stays just long enough to watch the grind hollow everything out. The novel turns shift work, hangovers, failed relationships, and bureaucratic absurdity into something surprisingly hard to put down.

Chinaski is endlessly watchable. The plot is loose and episodic, but the book moves fast because Bukowski never lingers where another writer might search for meaning. His prose is stripped down, mercilessly direct, and funny in a bleak, shrugging way.

Post Office feels like the natural companion to Ham on Rye, which shows how Chinaski was made. Post Office shows what happens after -- adulthood as endurance test. I think Ham on Rye barely comes out on top for me, but they succeed for completely different reasons.

As a modern cult classic, Post Office earns its reputation through raw honesty and a refusal to romanticize work or ambition. It captures the soul-crushing repetition of bureaucracy with sharp humor. Undoubtedly though, Bukowski’s abrasive worldview and deliberately crude voice will absolutely turn some readers away.

This lands at a solid 4/5 stars. It’s a book for when you want something cynical, funny, and brutally honest about work and survival, and don’t mind if it laughs at you along the way.

Title: Strange Pictures
Author: Uketsu
My Review:
Uketsu's Strange Pictures is a short, puzzle-like mystery built around eerie drawings and the unsettling stories behind them.

I'm not surprised this book has become so popular because the premise is genuinely fun and creative, and the creepy atmosphere works well. There are several moments that feel quietly unsettling and intriguing. It’s easy to read in a sitting, and the mystery element makes it very bingeable.

That said, I never found it particularly scary, and the story sometimes felt over-explained in a way that drained some of the mystery. The prose also felt fairly basic, which made the experience feel lighter than I expected from the premise.

Overall, I enjoyed my time with it, but it’s not one I’m rushing to recommend to everyone. A fun, creepy read that wasn't much of a standout for me.

Title: Wise Blood
Author: Flannery O'Connor
My Review:
Wise Blood follows Hazel Motes, a war veteran who returns to the American South determined to reject belief and start a “Church Without Christ,” only to become entangled with a cast of unforgettable misfits. It’s a cornerstone of Southern Gothic—grotesque, darkly comic, and deeply concerned with questions of belief, morality, and the human urge to find (or flee) meaning.

O’Connor’s genius is on full display here. I had to pick my jaw up off the floor more than once at how vividly and convincingly she brings these characters to life; they feel exaggerated and startlingly real at the same time. The novel is strange in the best way, fearless in its themes and unflinching in its vision. I instantly understood why this book is considered both a classic and a defining work of the Southern Gothic tradition.

Title: Atonement
Author: Ian McEwan
My Review:
Atonement is a literary novel about love, guilt, and the consequences of a single misunderstanding, set against the backdrop of pre- and post-World War II England.

It may appeal to readers who enjoy richly detailed settings, intricate social dynamics, and stories that explore moral complexity. McEwan’s writing is precise and elegant, and the novel is widely praised for its carefully structured narrative and its deep exploration of memory and the weight of past mistakes.

For me, however, it didn’t land. The story moved slowly in a way that felt tedious rather than immersive, and I struggled to connect with the characters or feel the tension of the central drama. While the descriptions of the English countryside and social hierarchy were beautiful, they didn’t draw me in emotionally. I can understand why the book is so highly regarded, but to me, the story felt dull, and I never quite got swept up in the narrative the way many readers do.

Title: Novelist as a Vocation
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
Novelist as a Vocation sits beautifully alongside the other “on writing” books I’ve loved by authors like Stephen King and Anne Lamott, yet it feels refreshingly distinct.

Murakami offers perspectives I’d argue only a Japanese writer, or one writing outside the U.S., could provide, from his unique approach to the craft to his insights on life. His methods and ways of thinking often diverge from what I’ve read elsewhere, making the advice feel both practical and original.

The one thing I wished for was a deeper dive into his personal life or childhood, which might have elevated the book even more. Still, Murakami comes across as humble, thoughtful, and genuinely helpful.

I'd say this is a must-read for any aspiring writer.

Title: A Season in Hell and The Drunken Boat
Author: Arthur Rimbaud
My Review: Rimbaud has flashes of incredible imagery that stick with you, but I often found myself lost in the poems, unsure what to make of them. Maybe it was the wrong book or the wrong moment, but I didn’t fully connect this time. I’m open to revisiting in the future because there’s clearly brilliance here, even if it didn’t fully click for me.

Title: Carl's Doomsday Scenario (Dungeon Crawler Carl, #2)
Author: Matt Dinniman

All in all, pleasantly surprised.

Title: The House on Mango Street
Author: Sandra Cisneros
My Review:
"There beneath the roots of soggy flowers were the bones of murdered pirates and dinosaurs, the eye of a unicorn turned to coal."

The House on Mango Street follows Esperanza, a young Latina girl growing up in a poor Chicago neighborhood, as she observes her family, her neighbors, and herself through a series of short, lyrical vignettes. Rather than a traditional plot, the book unfolds as a collage of moments, memories, and impressions, reading less like a conventional novel and more like poetry in prose.

Though the short chapters are loosely connected, they share a consistent tone and a powerful emotional throughline: yearning.

Esperanza longs for escape, for autonomy, for a room of her own and a future that does not simply repeat the lives of the women around her. Cisneros captures this with remarkable impact. A single page can carry the weight of an entire coming-of-age story, using fragments to build a deeply felt portrait of identity and place.

Within the landscape of modern classics, this sits comfortably alongside works like Autobiography of Red by Anne Carson or Bluets by Maggie Nelson, books that blur genre and prioritize voice, mood, and emotional truth over conventional structure.

This is a book for readers who are open to nontraditional storytelling and who enjoy literature driven by atmosphere rather than plot. It is especially good if you are in a reflective, quietly melancholic mood, or if you want something that can be read slowly, vignette by vignette. Cisneros gives a vivid sense of what it may have felt like to grow up impoverished and Hispanic in that time and place, without flattening her characters into symbols. Even when Esperanza observes pain, she does so with tenderness and clarity. Some of the most striking moments come from Esperanza’s unfiltered despair, like in this beautiful but devastating passage:

“I read somewhere in India there are priests who can will their heart to stop beating. I wanted to will my blood to stop, my heart to quit its pumping. I wanted to be dead, to turn into the rain, my eyes melt into the ground like two black snails. I wished and wished.”

The House on Mango Street helped expand what counted as a “novel” in American literature and made space for voices and lives long pushed to the margins. It is an emotionally resonant book that proves you do not need length or narrative complexity to leave a lasting mark.

Title: Slow Guillotine: A Novel (Zero Street Fiction)
Author: Teo Rivera-Dundas

Title: Vigil
Author: George Saunders
My Review:
When I heard Saunders was dragging us back into the afterlife I was FULLY prepared to have my brain scrambled and my soul lovingly drop-kicked into the abyss. I was expecting George to haunt me, confuse me, and spiritually yeet me into the void.

So...DID HE DO IT?!

Yep. Vigil is as explosive, playful, and darkly funny as I was expecting, while tackling some of Saunders’ favorite obsessions: corporate greed, capitalism, and the environmental costs of progress.

Reading Vigil's synopsis, you might worry this is just Lincoln in the Bardo all over again, but this is a very different ride. A woman ushers a dying oil company CEO into the afterlife, and the story feels more grounded yet expansive. The CEO insists he has nothing to regret, claiming “I lived big. The world is better for it.” That wild certainty drives the tension between self-delusion and the consequences we leave behind.

Vigil has an indie, experimental vibe, so in my opinion it is not a book guaranteed to please casual readers or anyone looking for a neat, comforting story. It rewards patience and curiosity. Readers willing to get lost in moral complexity, existential humor, and jarring narrative turns will find themselves fully immersed. The pacing alternates between quiet reflection and bursts of chaotic energy-- moments that especially shine in the audiobook (extraordinary performances!).

Saunders is fully in command of his craft. The book manages to be challenging, surprising, and disorienting without being exhausting. As long as you let go and let Saunders lead, it's a ride worth taking.

Title: The Last of Earth
Author: Deepa Anappara
My Review:
Thank you to Random House and NetGalley for the opportunity to read and review the e-ARC of The Last of Earth. All opinions are my own.

The Last of Earth is an introspective novel that explores grief, guilt, and ghosts. It unfolds through a dual narrative, following a man and a woman navigating loss from very different social and cultural positions.

The dual perspectives are one of the book’s strongest elements. The parallel storylines add contrast and allow the novel to examine its themes from both a male and female point of view. Memories, past selves, and unresolved losses form the ghosts that haunt the characters across both narratives, shaping how each moves through the world. This structure is compelling, especially in how it highlights the different ways loss is shaped by social position and personal history.

I also appreciated how much I learned about Tibetan culture through this novel. The cultural details add a richness that elevates the book beyond a standard grief narrative.

Personally, the novel’s pacing tested my patience. The narrative unfolds slowly, and while I appreciated the depth of interior reflection given to both main characters, the momentum often stalled. Although there was little about this novel that I actively disliked, the read felt longer than it actually is, and I sometimes struggled to stay engaged.

Overall, The Last of Earth struck me as a slightly above average literary novel that is thoughtful, well written, and thematically ambitious, but not one I am rushing to recommend widely. That said, it may be a rewarding read for those who value slower paced novels focused on mood, introspection, and thematic depth over narrative drive.

3.25/5 Stars

Title: To the Lighthouse
Author: Virginia Woolf
My Review:
Virginia Woolf captures something almost impossible here. The way time passes inside a mind. The way love, resentment, grief, and longing can coexist. The way a single afternoon can feel infinite, while ten years can vanish in a sentence.

To the Lighthouse permanently altered how I think about time, memory, and what a novel is capable of doing. Woolf is not interested in plot so much as perception, in how experience accumulates quietly and how meaning is shaped by what is felt rather than what is said.

The Ramsays are ordinary people, yet Woolf renders their inner lives with such precision that their smallest thoughts feel monumental. Mrs. Ramsay’s desire to hold things together, Mr. Ramsay’s hunger for intellectual validation, Lily Briscoe’s struggle to create something lasting in the face of doubt and loss. These ongoing tensions ripple through the novel.

Again and again, the book reveals that life’s most important moments are rarely the loud ones. Meaning is found in passing thoughts, half formed emotions, and the spaces between events. Woolf’s treatment of time makes this unmistakable, and she acknowledges how indifferently it moves on.

This is essential reading for anyone drawn to interiority, emotional subtlety, and modernist ambition. It belongs alongside works like Proust’s explorations of memory, yet it remains uniquely Woolf in its restraint and intimacy.

Title: Ham on Rye
Author: Charles Bukowski
My Review:
This book dares you to stop reading. You won’t.

Ham on Rye is bleak, pessimistic, disgusting, and somehow also a damn good read. It’s the kind of novel that makes you recoil and keep going anyway, which probably explains why no one has ever recommended Bukowski to me. It isn’t a book you press into someone’s hands.

Bukowski’s portrait of Henry Chinaski’s childhood is brutal, offering no comforting psychological explanation to tie anything up neatly. What makes it hit so hard is how little the book seems to care whether you sympathize with Chinaski at all. The indifferent narration paradoxically makes the suffering feel more real. Pain isn’t framed as formative or ennobling. It just is, leaving a worldview where survival replaces hope as the primary accomplishment.

Bukowski’s prose is fearless, funny in the ugliest way, and sharp-eyed about hypocrisy, masculinity, and institutional cruelty. The book understands how resentment forms long before it hardens into ideology.

In the landscape of modern classics, Ham on Rye feels like The Catcher in the Rye stripped of sentimentality and mercy. Where Salinger gives us alienation with a safety net, Bukowski removes it entirely.

I don’t think you’re meant to enjoy Ham on Rye as much as you are meant to feel its honesty. It tells the truth as Bukowski sees it, and that truth is ugly, funny, and disturbingly convincing.

Title: Of Time and the River: A Legend of Man's Hunger in His Youth

Title: Natural Beauty
Author: Ling Ling Huang
My Review:
Ling Ling Huang’s Natural Beauty is an ambitious, unsettling debut that blends literary fiction, speculative horror, and social critique.

The novel follows a young pianist whose life unravels after her parents’ health collapses, pushing her into an elite beauty and wellness world where perfection comes at increasingly disturbing costs.

While the plot itself is simple, the experience is not. Huang excels at atmosphere, delivering moments of visceral body horror that genuinely unsettled me (in a good way, mostly). Many scenes were effectively surprising because they juxtaposed the intimate with the grotesque.

Where the book works best is its exploration of the protagonist’s complicated relationship with her parents, shaped by love, obligation, resentment, and grief. The novel also raises compelling questions about bodily autonomy, perfectionism, assimilation, and identity, especially within the context of beauty culture and experimental science.

Still, the execution is uneven. The tone wobbles between horror, satire, and melodrama, and at times the emotional beats feel overplayed rather than earned. A few moments pulled me out of the story entirely. While I understood what the novel was reaching for, the protagonist’s behavior sometimes stretched credibility, making it difficult to stay fully invested in the emotional stakes.

Overall, I wish Huang had been able to better control and unify the many compelling ideas in a way that fully landed for me.

That said, if you’re in the mood for something uncomfortable, idea-driven, and a little messy (and you enjoy books like Severance or My Year of Rest and Relaxation) this may work for you.

I didn’t love Natural Beauty as much as Huang’s Immaculate Conception (start there!) but both works makes it clear she’s a writer worth watching, and I can’t wait to read whatever she writes next!

Title: Mona's Eyes
Author: Thomas Schlesser
My Review:
Book of the year 2025? No, B&N. Just…no.

Mona’s Eyes centers on a grandfather’s attempt to teach his granddaughter how to see deeply while she still can.

I won’t lie—this book can be a split experience. The narrative is intentionally spare, prioritizing reflection over momentum. For readers who love art, it may feel like comfort; for readers who love novels, frustration.

Early on, the story felt noticeably thin to me, and Mona’s precociousness paired with the book’s gentle, almost overly curated tone made parts of it feel a bit twee. I rolled my eyes more than once.

But somewhere along the way, my resistance softened.

What the book lacks in narrative drive, it makes up for in breadth and curiosity. I began to appreciate the wide-angle view of art history, the way artists and movements are placed in conversation, and especially the attention paid to why people make art and what they’re reaching toward when they do.

Once I stopped asking the book to be something it wasn’t, I found myself settling into it.

I’m left with mixed feelings. At times, Mona’s Eyes reads like an Art History 101 course in disguise. But it’s also a gentle celebration of beauty, creativity, and looking closely.

Mona’s Eyes may not satisfy if you’re craving a robust story, but if you’re willing to wander slowly through art and ideas, it offers quiet rewards.

Title: The Golovlyov Family

Title: Old School
Author: Tobias Wolff
My Review:
Did Tobias Wolff invent light academia?

Probably not. But Old School comes awfully close.

It’s a compact coming-of-age novel about literary ambition, class anxiety, and the myths young men build around genius. I can see echoes of novels like Stoner in Wolff’s approach: restrained, introspective, and focused on moral consequences rather than plot.

Set at an elite New England boarding school in the early 1960s, the story follows a scholarship student convinced that writing, and the company of great writers, could help him transcend his humble beginnings.

Wolff’s prose does a lot in very little space, and he’s especially skilled at capturing how shame and ambition blur together. The episodic structure, centered on visiting writers, mirrors the narrator’s gradual disillusionment.

The novel explores the cost of wanting something too badly, and how storytelling can become a form of self-deception. The ending, while conceptually sound, doesn’t quite deliver the emotional weight built up earlier. Still, Wolff leaves sharp insights into ambition, self-delusion, and the delicate line between aspiration and obsession.

Ultimately, Old School is a strong, thoughtful book that falls just short of greatness.

Title: Lightbreakers
Author: Aja Gabel
My Review:
Following quantum physicist Noah and artist Maya, Lightbreakers explores their separate journeys toward healing while touching on art, science, and time. I found the scientific concepts surprisingly accessible, and the evolution of Maya and Noah’s relationship was especially compelling.

There were a few moments that felt overly serious or dramatic, and occasionally lines that aimed for profundity came across as a little forced. I would have welcomed some comic relief to balance the weightier themes.

Still, I liked Lightbreakers more than I expected. It’s a beautifully written story about grief, memory, and love, with a thoughtful exploration of human connection.

Recommended for: readers who enjoy reflective, speculative fiction with emotional depth. Fans of The Time Traveler’s Wife or Sea of Tranquility may particularly appreciate this novel.

3.75/5 ⭐️

Title: Hot Wax
Author: M.L. Rio
My Review:
ML Rio does rock ‘n roll!

In Hot Wax, her prose is polished and confident, with a dry humor that often landed for me. The dual timelines add some structural interest and allow moments to echo each other in subtle ways. The book is enjoyable when it slows down and leans into observation rather than performance.

That said, I was disappointed I didn’t have more of a connection to the characters, though it’s hard to pinpoint why I didn’t. This could still be great for other readers, but, unfortunately, it’s not a book I’m going to be rushing out to recommend, and I don’t think it’s going to stick in my memory for very long.

Title: The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny
Author: Kiran Desai
My Review:
The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny follows two Indian American siblings navigating questions of belonging and identity in the U.S. and later in India. The novel explores what it means to feel culturally split and emotionally unmoored, no matter which country you are in.

I liked this more than I disliked it, but I also struggled with it. The book felt long, but I understand why Desai gave it so much space. She’s attempting a broad portrait of what it means to grow up between cultures, shaped by migration, class, money, art, and family obligation, but that ambition often comes at the expense of pacing.

The novel frequently shifts focus to side characters. While these sections are thematically relevant, I consciously felt pulled away from the main characters. I can see how this fragmentation reflects the experience of growing up between cultures, but the emotional payoff didn’t always land for me.

Where the book worked best was in its quieter, more intimate moments, especially the relationship between Sonia and the artist, which captured tensions around creativity, desire, and self-definition.

This is an ambitious, contemplative work that sits alongside a lot of recent literary fiction that’s interested in questions of belonging and what it means to build a life across cultures. Ultimately, I admired what it was trying to do more than I enjoyed reading it.

3.25/5 ⭐️

Title: The Bridge of San Luis Rey
Author: Thornton Wilder
My Review:
Written in 1927, The Bridge of San Luis Rey reflects Wilder’s interest in medieval morality plays, classical tragedy, and Catholic and Stoic moral philosophy.

The novel begins with a sudden tragedy and follows a priest who attempts to understand whether human lives are governed by fate or by chance. In pursuing this question, the book examines the lives of several interconnected characters.

Structurally, it often feels like Wilder reverse-engineered a philosophical problem and then built a series of short character studies around it. That approach didn’t fully work for me. Still, the novel is doing more than staging a simple fate-versus-chance debate. Beneath the surface, it argues that the meaning of a life cannot be measured by logic, morality, or outcome.

Wilder is especially interested in misdirected love. The relationships he portrays are often obsessive, performative, or unbalanced, revealing how devotion can become isolating rather than sustaining.

I didn’t personally connect with the tone or the prose, which felt distant and deliberately allegorical. At times it read more like a collection of moral tales than a fully immersive novel.

The book ultimately offers a clear spiritual conclusion about love and meaning. While I understand what Wilder is reaching for, the novel didn’t convince me emotionally.

That said, it’s easy to see why The Bridge of San Luis Rey resonated with readers in its time. In the aftermath of World War I, it offered reassurance that even random loss could be reconciled with meaning, without relying on punishment or moral accounting.

In that sense, it feels less like a novel and more like a spiritual artifact of its moment.

2.5/5 ⭐️

Title: Monstrilio
Author: Gerardo Sámano Córdova
My Review:
Monstrilio is a dark, tender, and gloriously unhinged meditation on grief that refuses to behave like a traditional grief narrative. It explores love after loss, and what happens when that love is allowed to curdle, mutate, and take on a life of its own.

The story follows a mother and aunt who, after an unspeakable tragedy, quite literally refuse to let go. What begins as an act of desperate devotion slowly becomes something unsettling. The novel asks uncomfortable questions. How much of grief is about honoring the dead, and how much is about soothing the living? When does love stop being love and become something monstrous?

What makes Monstrilio so compelling is its tonal balancing act. The book contains grotesque body horror yet it is also at times deeply emotional and sincere. The horror never feels gratuitous because it externalizes the interior experience of grief.

Beneath the strangeness is a deeply human story about family, identity, generational trauma, and the terror of loving something you cannot save.

This is not a book for readers looking for familiar comfort. Monstrilio is for those who appreciate literary horror, grief narratives that resist sentimentality, and stories that are willing to sit in moral ambiguity. It understands that grief can be a kind of monster if we refuse to let it die.

Trigger warnings:
Child death
Graphic depictions of grief
Body horror
Gore
Emotional abuse
Obsessive behavior
Self-harm themes (non-graphic)

If you are drawn to books that blur the line between literary fiction and horror and you are open to being unsettled in deeply emotional ways, this one is unforgettable.

Title: Crux
Author: Gabriel Tallent
My Review:
Thank you to Penguin Random House / Riverhead Books and NetGalley for the opportunity to read the advance reader copy of Crux in exchange for an honest review. All opinions are my own.

“I wanted a guarantee. But that’s not how it works. You find out by trying.”

That line captures the emotional heart of Crux, a novel that is as funny and tender as it is painfully honest.

Crux follows two longtime friends standing at a crossroads, trying to decide what kind of lives they are willing to live and what compromises they can survive.

What immediately stood out to me was the humor. Tallent's understanding of how people are funny with each other shines, and the banter on the page feels natural. The comedy becomes part of how the characters survive fear and uncertainty, and it never undercuts the seriousness of what the novel is doing.

Beneath that humor is an examination of meaning, ambition, and disillusionment. The book captures the dread of wasting your life, of grinding toward something you no longer believe in, and of realizing the world may not offer what you felt it promised.

Tallent renders the friendship at the center of Crux with emotional precision. I believed in it completely, and I cared deeply about both characters. Their interior lives are portrayed with sincerity. Their thoughts spiral, contradict themselves, and loop back in ways that feel true to how real minds work. Through this, the novel reveals how closely the desire to be exceptional is tied to the desire to be loved.

The book is steeped in climbing terminology, but the most important term is the titular one. A crux is the most difficult moment in a climb. The climbing metaphor that runs through the novel is especially effective, particularly when Tallent writes, “It’s cruxes that matter. The top is only a symbol.” The hardest moment, not the outcome, is what defines you.

Even as it wrestles with fear and uncertainty, the book feels funny, emotionally generous, and quietly hopeful, the kind of novel that leaves you reflective but satisfied.

Ultimately, Crux is about choosing to step into uncertainty without guarantees. It is about trying anyway and about making meaning rather than waiting for it to appear. That is what made this a five-star read for me. It felt true to friendship, to fear, to ambition, and to the terrifying freedom of realizing that no one is going to hand you meaning. You have to step into it yourself.

Recommended for readers who love character-driven literary fiction, sharp dialogue, and books that ask hard questions without offering easy answers.

Note: This novel contains themes of grief, child abuse, mental health struggles, substance use, and existential despair, all handled thoughtfully and with care.

Title: How to Hold Someone In Your Heart (Lost Souls, #2)

Title: A Single Man
Author: Christopher Isherwood
My Review:
Wait...what?!

A Single Man completely caught me off guard, and not just because I went into reading it blind. It starts out charming and then quietly slides into absurdity.

The novel follows George, a middle-aged man moving through a single day in LA after the death of his partner, Jim. Very little happens externally, but internally the book is buzzing with grief, desire, irritation, and razor-sharp social observation.

George’s voice is the book’s greatest strength. It’s dry, intelligent, funny, and painfully self-aware. At one point he thinks, “Yes, I am crazy. That is my secret; my strength,” a line that perfectly captures how Isherwood allows irony, defiance, and vulnerability to coexist. The narration balances detachment and emotional precision without tipping into sentimentality.

Structurally and tonally, this reminded me of Woolf's "Mrs. Dalloway"-- a book that compress a life’s worth of emotion into a narrow window of time and rely on interiority rather than plot. If you like literary fiction that feels controlled on the surface but emotionally volatile underneath, this is very much in that vein.

And, oh man, at the end of the novel, Isherwood doesn’t soften the landing at all. He goes out with a bang. The tonal shift may be abrupt and unsettling, but it works. Instead of offering comfort or closure, the novel insists on randomness, mortality, and the illusion of control. It’s the kind of ending that makes you pause and think, "wait—what just happened?" and then, slowly, "oh!".

A Single Man is smart, strange, and memorable. I’d recommend it to anyone who enjoy sharp narrative voices, character-driven literary fiction, and books that aren’t afraid to end on a dark or unexpected note.

Title: A Death in the Family (Vintage International)
Author: James Agee

Title: House Made of Dawn
Author: N. Scott Momaday
My Review:
House of Dawn is one of those novels you approach with a lot of respect before you even open it. As a cornerstone of the modern Native American literary canon (and the book often credited with launching the Native American Renaissance), it carries real historical and cultural weight. I absolutely understand why this book matters. I just didn’t fully connect with it as a reading experience.

House of Dawn follows Abel, a young Jemez Pueblo man returning home after serving in WWII. He’s deeply alienated from white America, from his community, and often from himself. The novel traces his fragmentation and gradual movement toward healing through ceremony, memory, and reconnection with land and tradition. It’s a story about displacement, trauma, and the difficulty of re-entering a world that no longer feels like it fits.

If you’re familiar with Leslie Marmon Silko’s Ceremony, you’ll notice a lot of parallels here. Both novels center on a Native American veteran returning home and grappling with the dislocation of war, the trauma of cultural disruption, and the struggle to reclaim identity through ritual and connection to the land. The thematic and structural similarities are striking, but I think I’d actually recommend Ceremony over House of Dawn for readers seeking a more immersive and emotionally resonant experience. That said, House of Dawn could serve as a useful precursor: reading it first can gently introduce the motifs and narrative style that Silko expands upon so powerfully.

Momaday’s spare, lyrical prose is undeniably beautiful, especially when describing landscape or ritual, though the abrupt shifts in time and perspective sometimes made scenes hard to follow—I often admired the sentences more than I fully grasped the story.

Abel himself remains more symbolic than intimate, and the loose, unevenly paced plot mirrors his dislocation but can feel disorienting, with some sections dragging and others rushing by. The novel relies heavily on description over dialogue, which works in moments of ceremony but adds to the distance between reader and character; when dialogue does appear, it’s stark and powerful, though brief. The ending, focused on ritual rather than resolution, feels thematically appropriate but emotionally muted.

Where House of Dawn truly shines is in its thematic depth: identity, colonial violence, masculinity, spiritual rupture, and the possibility of healing through tradition are all handled with care. The novel’s ambition and originality reshaped the literary landscape, opening doors for countless Indigenous writers who followed.

Overall, House of Dawn is a novel I respect but didn’t love. Its literary influence is undeniable, but I found it more intellectually compelling than emotionally absorbing.

Who I think this book is for:
Readers interested in Indigenous literature and novels that prioritize theme, symbolism, and atmosphere over plot. If you enjoy challenging, fragmented narratives and don’t mind some distance between yourself and the characters, this may resonate more strongly.

I’m glad I read House of Dawn, but it wasn’t quite the connection I hoped for.

⭐️ 2.75/5

Title: The Stranger in the Woods: The Extraordinary Story of the Last True Hermit
Author: Michael Finkel
My Review:
The Stranger in the Woods is much more than the true story of a man who lived alone in the Maine wilderness for decades. It seeks to explain why he abandoned his former life and becomes a meditation on solitude, meaning, restlessness, and the subtle sense that something essential is always missing in modern life. Yet the book reminds us that “life isn't about searching endlessly to find what's missing. It's about learning to live with the missing parts.”

I’ve always been fascinated by the concept of hermits and what motivates someone to choose isolation, and this book approaches that curiosity with nuance rather than judgment. It asks questions most of us avoid facing: when we are truly alone, with no audience and no one to perform for, who are we? Do we lose our identity? It challenges readers to examine their relationship with solitude, comfort, and the rhythms of daily life, and to consider how we navigate purpose, connection, and intentional living.

The Stranger in the Woods is a deeply absorbing read, one I know I’ll return to again and again. Though it is grounded in a single man’s life, it resonates universally, reframing solitude, reflection, and self-discovery in ways that feel urgently relevant today. This book doesn’t just tell a story—it changes the way you see your own.

This book is for readers who enjoy thoughtful nonfiction that includes philosophical questions. It's well worth your time if you’re drawn to books about the tension between modern life and inner stillness.

Title: The Dharma Bums
Author: Jack Kerouac
My Review:
“I wanted to...go off somewhere and find perfect solitude and look into the perfect emptiness of my mind and be completely neutral from any and all ideas."
“I saw that my life was a vast glowing empty page and I could do anything I wanted.”
"...I felt free and therefore I was free."

If you’ve only read On the Road, you’re missing out on Kerouac’s more mature, reflective work: The Dharma Bums. This is the Kerouac for readers drawn to nature writing, spiritual seeking, and the feeling of wanting less while wanting everything.

Where On the Road is velocity and appetite, The Dharma Bums slows down, and asks harder questions: how to live freely without becoming careless, how to seek enlightenment without abandoning joy, how to belong to the world without being owned by it.

Written in the late 1950s, at a moment when postwar America was accelerating toward conformity, consumerism, and Cold War anxiety, The Dharma Bums captures young people turning eastward, inward, and toward the natural world in search of meaning. Kerouac’s embrace of Zen Buddhism, environmental awareness, and voluntary simplicity would go on to shape the 1960s counterculture. In The Dharma Bums, this shift still feels intimate, provisional, and unresolved rather than ideological.

It belongs on the same shelf as books where the natural world is not a backdrop but a teacher, and where spiritual searching is inseparable from physical experience. There’s a clear throughline to Thoreau’s Walden, though Kerouac replaces solitude with friendship and transcendental calm with ecstatic, lived messiness.

Kerouac’s relationship to nature is expansive, overwhelming, and deeply emotional:

"The woods do that to you, they always look familiar, long lost, like the face of a long-dead relative, like a piece of forgotten song drifting across the water… most of all like golden eternities of past childhood or past manhood and all the living and the dying."

"Trails are like that: you're floating along in a Shakespearean Arden paradise and expect to see nymphs and fluteboys, then suddenly you're struggling in a hot broiling sun of hell in dust and nettles and poison oak...just like life."

In The Dharma Bums, Kerouac’s Buddhism is joyful, contradictory, and deeply human. The novel is about chosen poverty, friendship, art made without permission, faith without institutions, and the desire to touch something infinite while still wanting wine, laughter, and long conversations. Mountains are climbed. Stillness is practiced. Both matter.

What makes the book feel surprisingly modern is its resistance to certainty. Rather than offering answers, it documents a process: spiritual curiosity without dogma, community without hierarchy, freedom without a fixed destination. In that sense, it feels newly relevant in a contemporary moment marked by burnout, disillusionment, and a renewed hunger for meaning outside traditional structures.

Near the end of the novel, the narrator has clearly made progress toward the enlightenment he seeks:

"Standing on my head before bedtime on that rock roof of the moonlight I could indeed see that the earth was truly upsidedown and man a weird vain beetle full of strange ideas walking around upsidedown and boasting..."

But, in a Socratic spirit, he continues to ponder and ask questions:

"Suppose we suddenly wake up and see that what we thought to be this and that, ain't this and that at all?"
"Are we fallen angels who didn't want to believe that nothing is nothing and so were born to lose our loved ones and dear friends one by one and finally our own life, to see it proved?"

The point isn’t the answers, but the asking.

So, is The Dharma Bums perfect? No. It rambles and resists polish, but that looseness is the point. Like much of Kerouac’s best work, it isn’t interested in refinement so much as sincerity.

I finished it feeling lighter, lonelier, freer, and more awake. A book I’ll return to whenever I forget how to look at the sky. Five stars, no hesitation, and a rare book that leaves you feeling both emptied and full at once.

Title: A Canticle for Leibowitz (St. Leibowitz, #1)
Author: Walter M. Miller Jr.
My Review:
A Canticle for Leibowitz is a classic dystopian science fiction novel often praised for its ambition, philosophical depth, and originality.

The book is set in a post-apocalyptic future following a devastating nuclear war. Civilization has collapsed, and much of human knowledge has been lost or deliberately destroyed. Centuries later, a Catholic monastic order dedicates itself to preserving scraps of scientific and philosophical knowledge.

The book's central idea, knowledge preserved without understanding, is clever and memorable. Plus, the novel was ahead of its time in imagining nuclear annihilation as a recurring historical pattern rather than a one-time warning. In that sense, it feels comparable to Foundation (full transparency: I've only seen the Foundation series), another work more interested in systems and ideas than in individual characters.

So, right off the bat, I can say that the book immediately struck me as ambitious, philosophical, and original. So far, so good.

But, then the reader encounters the first major hurdle: structure. The book is divided into three sections, set hundreds of years apart, tracing humanity’s slow climb back toward technological advancement. I tried to remain emotionally invested as each section introduced an almost entirely new cast. But, rather than feeling like a sweeping generational saga, it felt more like a series of loosely connected philosophical vignettes.

Another challenge is the characters. The monks, in particular, blurred together for me, and much of the book reads as extended scholarly rambling. Yes, this is partly intentional, but it made large stretches feel static and difficult to engage with.

I couldn't help but compare the book to other dystopian novels like 1984, The Road, or Brave New World. Unfortunately, I found A Canticle for Leibowitz's apocalypse to be less compelling because it is mostly intellectualized rather than viscerally experienced, and the sense of emotional urgency felt muted. Though Miller is clearly interested in big concepts like faith versus reason and cyclical history, the story often tells about these themes instead of letting the reader feel them through character-driven stakes.

Even though I'm not the most avid science fiction reader, I had hoped I could still really get into A Canticle for Leibowitz. The harsh truth is that I appreciate what Miller is trying to do, and I found the central concept really interesting, but the execution did not work for me. Miller’s clean prose suits the material, but its dryness did little to pull me along. Combined with the slow pacing, the book often felt distant, meandering, and longer than it is.

I think I can confidently say that there are probably more ideal readers out there that Miller was targeting with this novel. Those who love idea-driven science fiction, religious allegory, and long-view historical speculation will find a lot to admire here.

But, still, I offer a warning to the average/casual reader-- don't pick up A Canticle for Leibowitz and expect to find a gripping dystopia with strong character development.

2.5/5 Stars

Title: Ceremony
Author: Leslie Marmon Silko
My Review:
Leslie Marmon Silko’s Ceremony is more than what it appears on the surface. It is a novel structured as a healing ritual. Once you see that, the book opens up in extraordinary ways.

Set in New Mexico, Ceremony follows Tayo, a mixed-race Laguna Pueblo man returning from WWII shattered by grief, survivor’s guilt, and the psychic violence of colonialism. He is haunted by memories of his cousin Rocky’s death, alienated from his community, and sick with something that cannot be explained as purely physical.

Silko braids Tayo’s narrative with Pueblo myth, poetry, and oral tradition, collapsing time so that ancient stories and contemporary trauma coexist. These mythic interludes do not interrupt the novel. They define its structure and reveal a central truth of the book: stories make the world, and broken stories can destroy it.

The novel’s wide cast of characters embody different responses to trauma and dislocation. Rage turned inward, self-destruction disguised as resistance, bravado used to mask despair, and shame inherited through generations all surface through the people Tayo encounters.

Silko’s prose is deceptively spare and carefully paced. The book demands patience and trust, rewarding readers who are willing to slow down and allow meaning to surface gradually.

You can feel Ceremony’s influence throughout Native American literature, from Louise Erdrich’s braided narratives to Tommy Orange’s collective voice. It also echoes the modernist fragmentation of Faulkner and the mythic layering of Toni Morrison, while remaining unmistakably its own.

At its core, Ceremony is a cosmological novel. It asks what happens when a people’s stories are interrupted, and how they might be repaired.

The novel’s quiet revelation is that tradition is not static. It adapts, or it dies. Healing requires new ceremonies for new wounds.

Why read Ceremony now? Because it shows that healing is not individualistic. Because it refuses the idea that progress requires forgetting. Because it insists that who tells stories, how stories change, and who stories exclude shape reality itself.

Who will love this book:
• Readers who value theme and structure over plot speed
• Fans of literary fiction, myth, and nonlinear storytelling

This was a four-star read for me, and it is easy to see why it is considered a classic. I will definitely be rereading Ceremony. There is simply too much here to absorb in one pass. The novel does not end when the last page does. Like any real ritual, it works on you quietly long after you have finished.

Title: The Art Thief: A True Story of Love, Crime, and a Dangerous Obsession
Author: Michael Finkel
My Review:
“He takes only works that stir him emotionally, and seldom the most valuable piece in a place. He feels no remorse when he steals because museums, in his deviant view, are really just prisons for art.”

In The Art Thief, I was fascinated to learn about bibliomania (an obsessive, sometimes compulsive craving to collect books or art objects) and about Stendhal syndrome, a real condition where people can experience dizziness, anxiety, or even fainting when confronted with overwhelming beauty. These ideas sit at the center of the story of Stéphane Breitwieser, who stole 239 artworks from 172 European museums between 1995 and 2001… not for profit, but out of pure, consuming admiration. At one point, he even describes his obsession with devastating simplicity: “Art is my drug.” (I need this on a t-shirt!)

Finkel’s prose is clean, fast, and almost novelistic (though with very little dialogue), which makes this wild spree incredibly readable. The tone stays curious rather than sensational, allowing Breitwieser’s audacity and his strange, intense relationship to beauty to carry the book.

It’s no surprise this was a Goodreads Choice Award Nominee for Readers’ Favorite Nonfiction (2023). The blend of true crime, psychology, and art history makes it both accessible and compelling, even for someone like me who isn’t a heavy nonfiction reader.

The Art Thief is engaging, fascinating, easy to recommend, and absolutely worth the read.
