Title: The Elements (The Elements, #1-4)
Author: John Boyne
My Review:
4.25/5 Stars

John Boyne’s The Elements is an ambitious exploration of guilt, trauma, complicity, and the possibility of redemption. Boyne links four novellas in which he follows a woman fleeing scandal, a young athlete on trial, a surgeon shaped by childhood wounds, and a father traveling with his son.

He writes with a controlled intensity that lets the emotional weight land without melodrama. The characters are deeply flawed yet rendered with empathy, and their private shame and fear often feel painfully close. One line captures the book’s raw honesty about the damage we carry:

“I used to think the past was a place I could outrun, but it waits for me everywhere I go.”

The connections among the four narratives are give the book a cumulative force. Still, the repetition of trauma and the increasingly tight coincidences can feel numbing by the final section.

This is a heavy read that does not look away from the realities of abuse, guilt, and the long fallout of silence, so emotional readiness is essential. Readers who appreciate the intensity of novels like A Little Life will find similar power here.

Overall, this is a challenging and gripping novel: unsettling, absorbing, and morally complex. Even in its darkest moments, The Elements offers small but meaningful glimpses of humanity.

Title: Play It As It Lays
Author: Joan Didion
My Review:
After hearing about the legendary Joan Didion for years, I worried my first experience reading her might not live up to the hype. Let me tell you, it absolutely did.

I expected the prose and the inventive form to impress, and they do. What I didn’t expect was the cold, unrelenting bleakness. Didion strings together spare sentences and clipped paragraphs into a pervasive sense of disquiet and detachment, all while maintaining a cinematic precision that makes every scene feel sharply lit and inescapably real.

Maria (pronounced mar-eye-uh) Wyeth is a former actress drifting through LA and Las Vegas in the aftermath of professional collapse and a disintegrating marriage. The novel unfolds in short, fragmentary chapters that slip backward and forward without neat cause-and-effect, amplifying its feeling of orbiting meaninglessness. That fractured structure mirrors Maria’s inner unraveling, and Didion’s L.A. becomes a hollow sprawl of freeways, motels, and casinos where glamour curdles into isolation and despair.

Didion’s control of tone is masterly. She creates a kind of intimate numbness: you feel the distance in Maria’s voice, but also the ache beneath it. Take a line like: “One thing in my defense, not that it matters: I know something Carter never knew, or Helene, or maybe you. I know what ‘nothing’ means, and keep on playing.” Maria keeps “playing” the game of life even when the rules feel void, and that tension gives the novel much of its power.

If you’re drawn to unsettling, psychologically rich novels like The Bell Jar or My Year of Rest and Relaxation, you may find Didion’s unique take on a woman’s mental unraveling deeply compelling. Just make sure to check trigger warnings because this is an unflinchingly bleak read.

4.25/5 stars

Title: Big Chief
Author: Jon Hickey
My Review:
At the surface, Big Chief is the tale of a tense reelection campaign for Tribal President, but underneath it’s the story of a man trying to understand where he belongs, within his community, his family, and even within himself.

Jon Hickey’s debut surprised me in the best way. I don’t usually enjoy politically focused novels, yet his writing pulled me in immediately. The prose is never showy, but it’s quietly powerful and commands your attention from the first pages.

Mitch Caddo, the protagonist, is in the middle of a profound period of self-discovery, confronting old wounds, tribal politics, personal loyalties, and the ghosts he’s avoided for far too long. Hickey brings you deep into Mitch’s internal world in a way that makes his guardedness feel earned, even empathetic. His voice is funny, cynical, bruised, and vulnerable all at once, creating a character you root for even when he’s pushing people away.

Hickey weaves humor and sharp sarcasm throughout the novel, balancing the darker themes with an ease that feels natural to Mitch’s perspective. Stylistically and emotionally, the book reminded me at times of Tommy Orange’s There There: a community under pressure, interwoven histories, and personal reckonings happening alongside political ones.

It impressed me how Hickey handles themes like sovereignty, corruption, activism, and belonging with nuance and without turning them into a lecture. The political backdrop raises the stakes, but the heart of the novel lies in the relationships. Their conflicts are intimate and deeply human, even as they unfold against protests, power plays, and a community on the brink of unraveling.

Hickey never loses sight of the characters’ inner lives. In the end, Big Chief becomes a story about trying to return to a people, to a home, and to a version of yourself you can actually live with.

Big Chief is one of the strongest works of literary fiction I’ve read from 2025 so far. I’ll be picking up whatever Hickey writes next, without a doubt!

Title: Down and Out in Paris and London
Author: George Orwell
My Review:
Down and Out in Paris and London is a vivid look at poverty in two great cities.

The Paris chapters plunge the reader into a frantic world of grimy, overheated restaurant kitchens, and Orwell captures the chaos with sharp detail. The London section shifts into the slow rhythm of tramp life, where days blur together and even basic survival becomes routine, echoing the spirit of Jack Black’s "You Can’t Win".

Orwell’s dry humor and eye for small absurdities keep the book lively. He is at his best when showing the strange mixture of camaraderie among workers bound by exhaustion and a shared lack of money, and the steady misery that comes with being broke.

For me, the book never fully comes together as a cohesive narrative. It reads more like a series of vivid but loosely connected sketches, and the social commentary, though interesting, often interrupts the flow instead of emerging naturally from the scenes. The book felt more journalistic than emotional, driven by observation rather than character or narrative momentum, which may appeal to readers who prefer raw experiential writing over traditional storytelling.

Despite its unevenness, this remains an engaging early work from Orwell. Readers interested in restaurant culture, social history, or Orwell’s development as a writer will find plenty to appreciate. For others, it may feel less than essential.

Author: Nathanael West

Title: The Mad Wife
Author: Meagan Church
My Review:
The Mad Wife is one of those novels that defies easy genre labels. It has suspense and a few surprising twists, but I wouldn’t call it a thriller; it brushes up against historical fiction and mystery, but doesn’t sit neatly in either category. To me, it is domestic literary fiction that offers a character-driven story about identity, resilience, and the quiet unraveling of a 1950s housewife under suffocating expectations.

What I enjoyed most was the psychological depth. Meagan Church digs into the emotional cost of being a “perfect” mid-century wife: the performative smiles, the repression, and the medical gaslighting disguised as concern. Lulu’s inner world is beautifully explored, and the novel gives her space to question not only the people around her but her own sense of reality. The prose is sharp and straightforward, with flashes of lyricism that really stayed with me, such as “All of us are evolutions of ourselves…” or “Life is a continual process of letting go…” which feel like the book pausing to breathe and reflect.

I loved that there were twists I didn’t see coming, but the book does not rely on shock. Instead, it builds a slow, creeping sense of dread that mirrors Lulu’s growing uncertainty. It explores themes many readers will relate to, including grief, imposter syndrome, and the masks we put on to survive, while grounding everything in a vivid sense of time and place.

Overall, The Mad Wife is an accessible yet impactful read that I think a wide range of readers could enjoy. It is haunting and memorable. Just be sure to check the trigger warnings before diving in.

Title: The Subtle Art of Folding Space
Author: John Chu

Title: Perfection
Author: Vincenzo Latronico
My Review: Vincenzo Latronico name-drops Animal Collective, vaporwave, and Helvetica Neue like he’s speed-running a Hipster Starter Pack. Perfection is 120 documentary-style pages (or a crisp 3-hour listen) of hipsters in their natural habitats: obsessing over aesthetics, curating their spaces, and quietly imploding under the weight of self-awareness. The concept may seem clever, but the total absence of dialogue or emotional heat leaves the whole thing feeling more like an art installation than a story.

Title: On the Calculation of Volume II
Author: Solvej Balle
My Review:
Tara dissociates; she slips from herself. As anyone trapped in a single repeating day might, she realizes she’s now confined to one season. So she sets out in search of the others. What follows is a wandering, meditative pilgrimage through space and history: she seeks winter, spring, and summer, and in the process she stumbles across everything from the internet to the Roman Empire.

This volume feels like Solvej Balle asking: What if Tara stops circling her own terror long enough to live? What would she notice? Who would she become? Tara’s thoughts drift, settle, and reform, and the pleasure of the novel lies almost entirely in inhabiting her interiority. Not much “happens,” but that’s intentional. It’s a study in what remains when life’s structure disappears.

I loved how expansive the world suddenly feels. The novel stretches outward while everything stays tethered to Tara’s consciousness. Her searching becomes a strange, lovely metaphor: a woman caught outside of time trying to gather all the seasons back into her hands.

And then there’s the final paragraph, which finally (finally!) nudges the series forward. It’s a small shift, but it lands like a cliffhanger. After so much stasis, that movement feels seismic.

On The Calculation of Volume, Book II is a hypnotic, thoughtful continuation that’s restrained, existential, and quietly bold. I’m already itching for Volume III.

4.25 ⭐️

Author: Elizabeth McCracken

Title: The Night Watchman
Author: Louise Erdrich
My Review:
I really tried with The Night Watchman and even pushed myself to finish it, hoping it would eventually click. But in the end, my main reaction was… indifference. I never quite connected with the characters, and the plot didn’t pull me in the way I expected. The writing, while clearly meaningful to many readers, just felt very average to me.

What makes this harder is that the subject matter is genuinely important. The fight against the termination Indigenous tribes is a powerful story, and one I wanted to be deeply moved by. I can see how this resonates for so many people, but for whatever reason, the emotional impact never fully landed for me.

I’m honestly a little surprised by how praised this book is, but reading is so personal. This one simply wasn’t for me, even though I appreciate the significance of the history it’s drawing from.

2.5/5 ⭐️

Title: Seasons of Glass and Iron: Stories
Author: Amal El-Mohtar

Title: Small Boat
Author: Vincent Delecroix
My Review:
Small Boat is one of those books that feels both fascinating and painful to read. I was struck by how deeply the author lets the reader inside the narrator’s head. It is almost unsettling at times, like being trapped in someone else’s conscience while they try to make sense of their own moral failures.

While the story centers on a tragedy in the English Channel, it is just as much about the psychology of rescue work, guilt, and the impossible ethics of deciding who gets saved and who does not. The book returns again and again to the unbearable truth that sometimes, even when someone is watching, help simply does not come.

The writing is sharp, philosophical, and at times almost dreamlike. Some passages read like moral poetry, especially when the narrator reflects on the sea and it becomes a character: ancient, indifferent, and a witness to every failure of human decency.

What stayed with me most is how the book explores the gap between intention and action. The narrator wrestles with the idea that most people want to believe they would say the words I will save you, even if they never step into the water. One line I kept returning to: “What mattered was not that they were saved; it was that I should be saved, and the whole world with me, through these words.” It is such a painfully accurate portrait of how we soothe ourselves with the idea of our own goodness.

Another moment that hit hard: “Even with their eyes shut, people are still watching… the stage is blacked out… they see nothing, but are still present at the drama.” The book stares straight at the uncomfortable truth that it is easier to feel moral than to be moral.

Small Boat is difficult, but never gratuitous. It is meant to be uncomfortable. The writing is astonishing—lyrical but never romanticized, raw without slipping into despair. I am genuinely glad I read it. It is one of the most thought-provoking books I have picked up this year.

4.5 stars, rounded up.

Title: The Appalachian Sea: Poems (Southern Messenger Poets)
Author: Steve Scafidi

Title: Old School Indian
Author: Aaron John Curtis
My Review:
Old School Indian is a thoughtful and distinctive debut, one where the voice carries you even when the plot does not fully come together.

Abe Jacobs, a forty-three-year-old Mohawk man, returns to his reservation for a traditional healing while facing a serious illness. The trip forces him to confront his past, his family, his relationships, and the identity he has kept at a distance for decades. Curtis gives Abe a sharp, funny, restless narrative style that hooked me right away. Even when the story wandered, the voice stayed engaging. The presence of his alter-ego, Dominick Deer Woods, adds an extra layer of texture. Curtis is fearless in the way he plays with structure, memory, and tone, and that inventive approach is one of the book’s strongest qualities.

The plot itself felt scattered. Abe comes home because he is dying and hoping his great uncle can help, but the novel spends much of its time inside Abe’s head as he revisits past relationships, especially his marriage to Alex. That focus sometimes made the forward momentum feel thin. Still, Curtis brings a vivid sense of culture, history, and emotional tension to the page. The humor and linguistic playfulness kept the reading experience enjoyable even when the story felt uneven.

The novel tackles big themes with sincerity: generational trauma, belonging, and what it means to come home after years away. The cultural grounding and emotional transparency give the story its force, even when the structure wobbles.

Overall, I am glad I read it, but it is not one I am rushing to recommend. For me it landed at a solid 3 out of 5 stars. Curtis has an incredible voice and a willingness to take creative risks, and I will definitely be curious to see what he writes next.

Title: Ruins
Author: Amy   Taylor
My Review:
Thank you to Random House / The Dial Press for providing access to this title through NetGalley. The following review reflects my honest and personal opinions.

Ruins by Amy Taylor follows a couple whose relationship is tested in unexpected ways against the sun-drenched backdrop of Athens, Greece. Emma is searching for meaning beyond work or motherhood, while Julian is grappling with the fallout of his stalled academic career. Things become complicated when they meet a young Greek woman named Lena.

Taylor excels at creating atmosphere. The novel is taut with emotional and psychological tension. Desire, power, and unspoken insecurities are subtly woven into the narrative. The writing is accessible yet literary, drawing readers into the characters’ morally complex world.

A clever element of the story is Emma’s reading of Medea. The play’s themes of betrayal, desire, and the consequences of morally fraught decisions echo the tensions in Emma, Julian, and Lena’s relationships. It highlights how passion and danger can coexist, and adds an extra layer of resonance to the unfolding drama.

The pace is slow to medium, particularly in the first half, as Taylor carefully establishes the characters’ motivations and backstories. I didn’t find the main characters particularly loveable, but their flaws felt realistic and thought-provoking. The story examines desire, intimacy, and human fallibility in a nuanced and insightful way.

The novel becomes more engaging once the stakes rise and the drama escalates. Emma’s introspection, Julian’s inner conflict, and Lena’s struggle with agency keep the narrative absorbing, even when morally ambiguous.

A “one year later” chapter offers reflection and closure, neatly tying together events and examining the ripple effects of choices.

Overall, Ruins was engaging, even if it wasn’t a perfect match for my personal tastes and suffered slightly from uneven pacing. I’d give it 3.5 out of 5 stars (rounded up to 4). Fans of literary fiction that examines flawed, morally complex characters, power dynamics, and emotional tension will find it satisfying.

Title: The True True Story of Raja the Gullible (and His Mother)
Author: Rabih Alameddine

Author: Robin Wall Kimmerer

Title: Atlas of Unknowable Things
Author: McCormick Templeman
My Review:
Thank you to St. Martin's Press for providing this book for review consideration via NetGalley. All opinions are my own.

Atlas of Unknowable Things sets out with an irresistible premise: a modern gothic mystery set high in the Rocky Mountains at secluded Hildegard College. Historian Robin Quain arrives for a prestigious residency, seemingly to study ancient manuscripts, but privately determined to uncover a mysterious artifact.

From the outset, the atmospheric strangeness hooked me: strange sounds over the lake, flickering lights between the pines, and faculty members who feel just a shade too polished to be real. Without spoiling anything, it was interesting to follow Robin's shift in perspective as curiosity overtook fear and she felt she might finally be at the center of something meaningful.

Templeman excels in the novel’s imaginative blend of historical detail, botanical lore, and occult intrigue. The setting is lush, inventive, and often the strongest part of the experience.

Where the book faltered for me was in its character work and dialogue. Several lines undercut the carefully crafted atmosphere. A moment like, “he tried to give me handsome-boy sad eyes, but I wasn’t falling for it. Looks only counted for so much” pulled me straight out of the tension. For a story steeped in gothic unease, many character interactions felt too forced or self-conscious to sustain the mood.

The plot hinges on Robin uncovering Hildegard’s secrets, and while the early breadcrumbs were intriguing, her later limitations didn’t feel organic or make a lot of narrative sense.

My frustration with her lack of progress peaked when Robin finally voices the exact question I’d been asking: why is she still here? She recognizes that the situation has tipped from intriguing into outright disorienting and even considers leaving. Up to that moment, the book had been building toward the importance of her discoveries, only to undercut itself with an abrupt shift that made the momentum feel squandered. It left me with the sense that the plot was pulling back the curtain simply to reveal a shrug.

By the end, Robin breaks the fourth wall and addresses the reader directly. I won’t give away what she says, but it’s an interesting thematic gesture that points toward the slipperiness of truth, perception, and the stories we tell ourselves. In practice, though, it didn’t fully smooth over the unevenness I felt in the novel’s middle.

For me, this was an engaging premise with flashes of brilliance, but the inconsistent character dynamics and narrative choices kept it from fully landing. I rate it 2.75 stars, rounded up to 3. That said, I would still recommend it to readers who love enigmatic academic settings, metafictional twists, and stories where atmosphere takes precedence over clarity. Fans of modern gothic mysteries may be more satisfied than I was with the novel’s ambition, experimental structure, and eerie campus vibes.

Title: Knife: Meditations After an Attempted Murder
Author: Salman Rushdie
My Review:
Knife is a deeply personal and searing memoir in which Rushdie recounts the 2022 knife attack, his long physical recovery, and the emotional aftermath.

He writes with wit, urgency, and unflinching honesty. This is far more than a record of trauma. It is a meditation on survival, love, art, and the power of creativity in the face of violence.

This book is for anyone who believes in art as a way to make sense of the unthinkable. It is a testament to resilience, freedom of expression, and the redemptive power of writing.

Title: What I Talk About When I Talk About Running
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
“Pain is inevitable, suffering is optional.”

In this deceptively simple memoir, Murakami reflects on the irrepressible link between his writing life and his passion for running. He writes candidly about preparing for marathons, training alone, and the strange, meditative space you enter while running. The book feels like philosophy in motion in that Murakami reveals that running isn’t just physical training, but a metaphor for endurance, creativity, and the solitary craft of writing.

If you're into running, writing, or just curious about the discipline behind creativity, this memoir offers a quietly powerful portrait of what it takes to keep going, mile after mile, word after word.

Title: Bird by Bird: Some Instructions on Writing and Life
Author: Anne Lamott
My Review:
Bird by Bird is equal parts writer’s manual and heart-to-heart pep talk. Lamott’s voice is warm, funny, and unfiltered, full of hilarious stories about family, faith, and the painful, beautiful chaos of putting words on the page. It's easy to enjoy the raw honesty of her advice, such as “tell the truth … risk being unliked”, and how she nudges you to write even when you don’t feel ready.

Whether you’re a seasoned writer or just someone who dreams of starting, Bird by Bird reminds you that writing is messy and slow, and that’s okay! It teaches you to take things one “bird” at a time, with courage, grace, and humor.

Title: Valuable Humans in Transit and Other Stories
Author: qntm

Title: The Devil Is a Southpaw
Author: Brandon Hobson
My Review:
A challenging but unexpectedly addicting read.

It feels like this novel should come with a disclaimer: Don’t expect to feel in control—let the narrator’s obsession and passion wash over you. The flowery, hypnotic language is part of the experience, not an obstacle.

Hobson strikes a sharp balance between visceral, propulsive prose and a plot that simmers in a dark, mysterious atmosphere. The result is a slow, immersive burn that echoes in your thoughts afterward.

4.25/5

Title: Immaculate Conception
Author: Ling Ling Huang
My Review:
If you like literary-speculative fiction that blurs art, obsession, and technology, this one’s worth checking out. It follows Enka, a struggling artist who becomes entangled with the dazzling Mathilde, and explores the possibilities of a new technology called the Scaffold that links minds in the name of empathy and creative collaboration. The result is part art-world fever dream, part psychological thriller, paced like a slow burn that builds to something raw and unnerving.

This book teetered right on the edge of me really liking it. While the razor-sharp writing and blistering emotions had me devouring the novel in only a few sittings, the Scaffold concept and the way Enka connects her mind with Mathilde felt contrived, a little too gimmicky. Still, Huang’s prose and emotional insight nearly overcame that. The psychology at play was fascinating, and I enjoyed seeing how easily admiration blurs into fixation, and good intentions curdle into something murkier. I loved watching their friendship evolve from awe to dependency to quiet destruction. The art scenes and Enka’s hunger to be great grounded the book in something painfully human.

What stuck with me most was the tension between devotion and desire, and how ambition can corrode empathy. The mind-link premise sometimes veered into cringe territory, but Huang always reeled it back with beautiful, devastating clarity. I was frequently caught between fascination and discomfort, in a wonderful way.

I rate Immaculate Conception a 3.75/5 because it’s a fearless, unnerving exploration of art, envy, and identity, but it didn’t win me over completely.

Title: Shadow Ticket
Author: Thomas Pynchon
My Review:
I went into Shadow Ticket with high hopes. I’m glad to say I had fun with it!

Milwaukee, 1932. Private-eye Hicks McTaggart thinks he’s found stability and job security until he’s assigned to track down the heiress of a Wisconsin cheese fortune who’s wandered off. The search goes transatlantic, and Hicks ends up in Hungary, chasing more than a missing woman while crossing paths with Nazis, Soviet agents, British spies, outlaw bikers, jazz musicians, and paranormal knacksters.

On the surface, it’s a rollicking detective caper full of absurd turns and vintage style. Beneath that playful shell lies Pynchon’s continuing obsession with unraveling the myth of individual agency in the face of sprawling systems like capitalism, fascism, and espionage. The detective doesn’t so much solve the case as drift through it while the ground gives way beneath him, suggesting that knowledge accumulates faster than meaning. In our current state of global disinformation, rising authoritarianism, and bizarre conspiracies, Hicks’s Lindy-hop through chaos feels oddly timely. He’s not heroic; he’s just trying not to trip. Character-wise, Hicks is unique and likable. His past as a strikebreaker and his moral unease are there, but the focus remains more on the world around him than on his inner life.

As for the title: a “ticket” refers to a case assignment given to a gumshoe, or his reason to exist within the system. The “shadow” part echoes both the literal noir tone and a historical reference to Hungary’s so-called “shadow region,” an area caught between empires and ideologies. Together, Shadow Ticket hints at a mission through murky borders, where the line between reality and paranoia blurs and even one’s sense of purpose becomes suspect.

This is vintage Pynchon: secret organizations, weird phenomena, song lyrics tucked into dialogue, conspiracies riffing into absurdity. It feels like Pynchon having fun while still keeping his thematic backbone intact. Whether you rank Shadow Ticket among his best or not, it’s a reminder that no one else writes like him.

Of course, there’s plenty here to please longtime Pynch-heads, but die-hards may feel the darker depths of paranoia and the labyrinthine digressions of earlier years are slightly muted. If you wanted another Gravity’s Rainbow or expected Pynchon to reinvent himself entirely, you might come away disappointed.

If you’re in the mood for something joyously eccentric, richly layered with historical oddities, jazzy detective drama, and cheese conspiracies, this book delivers. It’s buoyant, imaginative, and full of sentences that make you grin mid-page. The pacing moves from a smooth detective-lounge opening into a free-fall of conjured locations and surreal shifts. Don’t expect a steady gear change...expect a tumble!

A small PSA for those new to Pynchon: if you’re expecting tight plotting, deeply defined characters, or a firm central message, you might get frustrated. Sometimes the weirdness overwhelms coherence, but remember, feeling untethered is half the fun!

Title: Flesh
Author: David Szalay
My Review:
Shortlisted for the Booker Prize 2025, Flesh follows a Hungarian man whose life is marked from adolescence by a disturbing sexual relationship that shapes how he relates to others and drifts through the world.

The first section hooked me. The writing is taut and unsettling, and I kept thinking, "where is this going"? Well into the book I was still wondering. And THEN, I realized, "oh, it’s one of those books". Szalay uses a “life told in moments” structure: instead of dramatic peaks, we get a steady drip of experience, movement, and feeling. The plot focuses less on dramatic change than on accumulated experience, drift through different social strata, and the body’s and psyche’s quiet response to events. Once I understood that, the novel’s shape made sense, even if it still left me slightly adrift.

István is a difficult protagonist to connect with. He moves through life passively, with things happening to him rather than because of him, and his emotional flatness can be frustrating. Yet the book’s strength lies in tracing how his early trauma ripples through later relationships, and how the body holds what the mind cannot articulate. The title becomes its thesis: the body (flesh) is a metaphor for where trauma happens, desire shows up, status is carried, and aging betrays.

Even the cover reinforces these themes: an apple core revealing the silhouettes of two people, a striking image of what’s been consumed and what remains, and how human connection exists in hollowed-out spaces. It mirrors a story preoccupied with what endures after damage, and what’s left once everything essential has been stripped away.

Ultimately, Flesh is spare, haunting, and occasionally brilliant. It’s an introspective study of damage, disconnection, and the ways early trauma shapes a life, and while it didn’t fully grip me emotionally, I appreciate the depth of its themes and the precision of Szalay’s writing.

Though I’m torn on the rating and it could easily be a 3.5, I’m going with 3 because it more accurately reflects how much I enjoyed the book.

Title: A Month in the Country
Author: J.L. Carr
My Review:
A shell-shocked veteran of WWI is hired to uncover a medieval mural in a Yorkshire church, where he finds quiet healing.

I found this short novel gentle and atmospheric. Carr captures the slow rhythms of rural life and the sense of time suspended after trauma. The restoration of the mural mirrors the protagonist’s own recovery, and his interactions with the vicar’s wife add just enough tension to the stillness.

Some readers may find this understated story undeniably beautiful but also missing the emotional swell that might have made it truly unforgettable. Still, there’s much to admire here: the prose is spare but luminous, and every scene hums with warmth and melancholy.

A Month in the Country is a solid read for anyone who enjoys quiet, pastoral fiction about healing, art, and the gentle passage of time.

Title: Chess Story
Author: Stefan Zweig
Additional Authors: Peter Gay, Joel Rotenberg, Стефан Цвайг
My Review:
Chess Story is a concise, psychologically sharp novella about obsession, memory, and the strange hold a game can have over the mind. On a ship to Buenos Aires, a world-champion chess player crosses paths with an unlikely opponent, and what begins as a simple match pulls into deeper territory. Chess becomes more than a game, and thinking turns inward in unsettling ways.

Zweig writes with precision and restraint; every page feels purposeful. Even as someone who already loves chess, I appreciated how the book captures both the thrill of the game and the claustrophobia of over-thinking it.

The ending is abrupt and left me wanting a bit more, but it feels in keeping with the book’s focus on psychological tension over tidy resolution.

Chess Story is a short, thoughtful, and quietly gripping read that sits with you after you finish it.

Title: On the Calculation of Volume I
Author: Solvej Balle
My Review:
Time could break. On The Calculation of Volume I is a haunting exploration of that possibility. Many of us are already ruled by the clock, but this novel asks who we are when we truly become prisoners of time.

I found myself drawn into the protagonist Tara’s inner life: her loneliness, the creeping sense of isolation as everything repeats and nothing changes, her hope that something might shift, her despair when it doesn’t.

Tara’s loneliness, her yearning for meaning, the slow drift away from her husband Thomas are all rendered with startling realism.

This story has done a fantastic job of setting the stage and mood for a series, one that I’m now totally invested in continuing!

Overall, this was a quiet and slow but profound read. I found myself savoring its blend of a speculative concept with emotional intimacy.

4.5/5

Title: I Gave You Eyes and You Looked Toward Darkness
Author: Irene Solà

Title: Hungerstone
Author: Kat Dunn
My Review:
In Hungerstone, Kat Dunn invites us into a richly textured world of gothic dread, creeping desire, and waking rage. I’d say the novel is not quite a retelling Carmilla but it is at least strongly inspired by it. What to expect: a woman starved of autonomy, a mysterious guest who upends everything, and a slow-burn journey toward self-recognition and reckoning.

The good: the atmosphere is mesmerising, Dunn’s prose is sharp, and Lenore’s character arc is a fascinating spiral with a satisfying conclusion.

The bad: the pace bogs down a bit in the middle because the suspense drags on a little bit too long. Even so, I was still pulled forward to the ending!

Hungerstone may not satisfy every appetite (if you expected full-on vampire romance or break-neck horror), but if you want something mysterious, creepy, taut with tension, and grounded in female awakening, it’s a strong choice. I’d recommend it to someone looking for gothic mood over pure shock, atmosphere over constant action.

Title: The Ship of Theseus
Author: Garry  Harper
My Review:
Thanks to Garry Harper for the opportunity to read The Ship of Theseus (I read Version 0.1).

From projecttheseus.com:

“Just as Pablo chases perfection in his artwork, the novel itself will likewise continue to be refined and reimagined over time. Every few months, a new, free update will take the place of the last. Plot points may change, characters may come and go, the very form and structure altered and experimented upon. Each version is designed to stand alone, yet together they form a living, breathing work — gradually transforming into something completely different from where it all began.”

It’s a fascinating premise, though not what first drew me in. When I came across The Ship of Theseus, I completely missed its “evolution” aspect—I likely entered the giveaway because I’m a sucker for novels about artists, especially those on the verge of unraveling. I was very happy to win the free e-book :)

First off, Harper assumes the reader is familiar with the ancient thought experiment that asks whether an object that has had all its components replaced remains the same object. His protagonist, Pablo Navarre, embodies that paradox: a celebrated sculptor now jaded and cynical, riddled with imposter syndrome, desperate to break free from critics, collectors, and his own perfectionism. He wants to create the purest artistic representation of creation itself and, in doing so, reinvent himself.

There’s plenty here for readers drawn to meditations on identity, perfectionism, and the creative process. The novel oscillates between self-aware satire of the art world and moments of existential despair. Harper’s prose is sharp and playful, able to shift from sardonic to soulful in a single paragraph.

That said, Navarre’s reinvention feels somewhat limited. It hinges mainly on a few encounters with friends/colleagues, a homeless artist, and some drug-induced visions. There are brief flashes of emotional intimacy in his strained marriage to Jeanette, but it feels like Harper missed the boat (pun intended, haha) on exploring that realm more deeply. At times, I found myself unsure whether I empathized with Pablo at all. The bottom line: the art-world satire is biting and entertaining, but it occasionally overshadows the human drama.

Now, to address the elephant in the room: Harper’s plan to continually update the novel is ambitious, but is it practical? Or even necessary? It’s an inventive nod to the Ship of Theseus paradox, but I’m not yet convinced readers will feel compelled to revisit the book multiple times to track its transformations. Whether this ongoing reinvention enriches the experience or serves as a clever gimmick remains to be seen.

Final verdict: The Ship of Theseus kept me turning pages, even if it didn’t probe as deeply into Navarre’s core as I hoped. For me, his personal evolution doesn’t quite mirror the meta-reinvention of the novel itself (at least not yet) but that might change in future versions. As a first iteration, this is a promising, thought-provoking start that raises more questions than it answers.

3.5 / 5 stars, rounded up.

Title: Eileen
Author: Ottessa Moshfegh
My Review:
After devouring my third Moshfegh book, I can confidently declare myself a full-fledged fanboy. Eileen isn't flawless—it's a slow burn that could've shed a few pages—but the grotesque, unsettling world Moshfegh crafts is so compelling that I couldn't look away. Her writing is like a fever dream where every sentence feels both alien and intimately familiar.

Eileen Dunlop, the protagonist, is a masterclass in unreliable narration. Her observations are sharp, yet there's a palpable distance between her and the world around her. She describes herself as "not fundamentally unattractive... just invisible," capturing that haunting sense of being overlooked yet hyper-aware of every slight.

The pacing of Eileen may test some readers, but for those attuned to Moshfegh's rhythm, it's a rewarding descent into a mind both repellent and magnetic. The tension builds slowly, culminating in a climax that is as shocking as it is inevitable.

Eileen is a testament to Moshfegh's unparalleled ability to explore the grotesque facets of human nature. Moshfegh's prose is rich with discomfort, and the novel has a pervasive sense of unease and the protagonist's introspective paranoia. If you're ready to confront the uncomfortable truths about humanity, this novel is a compelling invitation!

Rating: 3.5/5, rounded up

Title: Buckeye
Author: Patrick Ryan
My Review:
“Sometimes the stories we tell ourselves about family are truer than the ones we live.”

Patrick Ryan’s Buckeye is both sprawling and intimate, like sitting down with someone’s entire family history and realizing it’s also, somehow, your own.

The scope is epic: parents, kids, generations crossing paths, secrets kept and unearthed. Ryan shows how family legacies ripple outward and inward, shaping children long before they understand the weight of what’s been passed down.

The novel’s straightforward prose strikes emotional chords that sneak up on you. One moment you’re reading along easily; the next you’re gutted by a line that rings with truth. Ryan captures the everyday ache of being human: the longing to be seen, the fragility of connection, the small moments where ordinary life becomes extraordinary.

Buckeye belongs on the shelf beside Elizabeth Strout and Ann Patchett. Like them, Ryan blends clean prose, deeply drawn characters, and an emotional core that cuts across age, gender, and background. He reminds us that “family drama” isn’t small—it’s the stage where our most universal struggles play out.

If I had to sum it up: Buckeye is a novel about the human condition in all its contradictions—loneliness and intimacy, fear and bravery, disappointment and love. For that reason, I’d recommend it widely. It’s a novel that makes you feel, and no matter who you are, there’s a good chance you’ll find a piece of yourself in it.

Title: This House Isn't Haunted But We Are
Author: Stephen  Howard

Title: Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark
Author: Alvin Schwartz

Title: Too Loud a Solitude
Author: Bohumil Hrabal
My Review:
“For thirty-five years now I’ve been compacting wastepaper, and I love it more than anything.”

That’s how we meet Hanta, a man who spends his life crushing books and papers into bales in a Prague cellar, and somehow, Hrabal makes it riveting.

On paper, this should be boring: one man, a hydraulic press, endless piles of books. But Too Loud a Solitude is a deceptively slim, quietly explosive meditation on knowledge, memory, censorship, and the strange tenderness of destruction.

Hanta is quirky, eccentric, sometimes grotesque, sometimes funny. He drinks beer by the gallon, converses with mice, daydreams of philosophers, and tenderly presses volumes of Kant, Hegel, and Lao-tzu into bales that become “more beautiful than bouquets of flowers.” His voice is unforgettable: half-rant, half-philosophical confession, tinged with melancholy.

It’s also one of the most original entries into the “books about books” canon. Hrabal captures the contradictory act of loving literature while destroying it, making Hanta’s underground existence a metaphor for intellectual repression in communist Czechoslovakia. The novel turns recycling into a metaphor for how ideas live, die, and resurface.

A memorable line:
“Because when you read too many books you see that man cannot accomplish much, and you learn to be humble.”

That’s Hrabal’s gift: aphorisms that sneak up on you, both disarming and profound.

That said, a couple caveats: the novel is rambling and repetitive by design. Hanta circles back on himself, drunk on words and beer. Some readers will find the stream-of-consciousness style tiresome. It’s not a conventional plot but a voice, a mood. If you need a tight story, this isn’t it. But if you surrender to Hanta’s odd, obsessive monologue, it’s strangely exhilarating.

At barely 100 pages, it’s the kind of book you can read in an afternoon. Hrabal's novella is quirky, tragicomic, deeply humane. It feels like a love letter to literature written in the shadow of its destruction.

Title: Vineland
Author: Thomas Pynchon
My Review:
I just finished Vineland and I have to admit that I struggled with it. The novel is often described as Pynchon’s “easiest” or “lightest” work, but I still found myself lost in its endless digressions, packed with jokes, side characters, and TV references. Supposedly stoner-hilarious, but for me, it felt more like noise than comedy.

Still, once I zoom out, I can see the shape of the story. At its heart, Vineland is about the fallout of the 1960s counterculture as it runs headlong into the paranoia and repression of 1980s America. A teenage girl tries to learn the truth about her absent mother, a hippie dad just wants to keep life together in northern California, and a slick government man symbolizes the creeping fascism that turns rebellion into sellout. The personal story mirrors the political one: what happens when a generation that promised freedom ends up fractured, compromised, or bought off?

Reading it feels less like following a plot and more like channel-surfing a strange late-night cable feed. You’ll stumble across:
• a man who annually has to jump through a plate-glass window to keep collecting his government check,
• ghostlike “Thanatoids” who mostly sit around watching television in a kind of limbo,
• meandering riffs on martial arts movies, Ronald Reagan, FBI surveillance, and stoner culture,
• and sentences so packed with pop culture references they almost collapse under their own weight.

If you vibe with that kaleidoscopic style, the novel can be a blast — equal parts satire, elegy, and absurdist cartoon. If not, it can feel like a haze you’re waiting to clear.

For me, Vineland didn’t quite resonate. But I can appreciate the big picture: a paranoid, goofy, sometimes moving look at how the dreams of the ‘60s dissolved into the neon glow of the ‘80s.

2.5/5 rounded up because it’s not for me, but I can see why it’s beloved by Pynchon fans.

Title: The Friend
Author: Sigrid Nunez
My Review:
From the moment I put down Sigrid Nunez’s The Friend, I felt like I had been let in on something quiet yet enormous. It’s deeply intimate and relatable. The narrator has a voice that sounds like it’s speaking to you, under the hum of loss, the roar of silence.

Nunez doesn't just give readers a story of a death, but a study in what remains and the way one’s life continues to echo. The narrator’s best friend and mentor has committed suicide, and she inherits his Great Dane, Apollo. Apollo ends up being shared grief, a catalyst for introspection, and a companion in silence.

At its core, the book dares to suggest that our losses define us:

“What we miss—what we lose and what we mourn—isn’t it this that makes us who, deep down, we truly are?”

Nunez uses the narrator’s writing life as a framework for the novel so that it feels part memoir, part essay, part love letter to literature. References to authors, reflections on what writing means, and how authors and readers relate to each other enrich it.

The tone is balanced between humor and heartbreak. Nunez has the uncanny ability to be both funny and tragic, to convey dry wit and emotional truth simultaneously. The narrator is self-aware, cleverly critical, able to mock literary pretensions one moment, and then in the next, stripped bare by grief.

The Friend is a novel that avoids clichés and that succinctly conveys how writing is one of the means we use to carry grief. Some readers may find The Friend to be too loosely structured, the sections about writing life long or digressive. That’s because the novel is more about ruminations, memory, emotional logic than narrative logic. It’s quiet rather than explosive—a novel that stays with you.

If you want your novels intimate, philosophical, raw but not overblown, this is one to read. It delivers beautifully in voice, in tone, in the small heartbreaks that echo large. It's deeply moving, exceptionally well crafted, and one of the most honest, resonant literary novels I’ve read in a while.

Title: Butcher's Crossing
Author: John  Williams
My Review:
Will Andrews walks away from Harvard and civilization and heads into the wilderness. What begins as a young man’s escape from academia soon becomes something far deeper: a search for self. When he joins a buffalo hunt, it isn’t just an adventure — it’s an initiation. From that point on, it’s Andrews vs. himself. Andrews vs. ideals. Andrews vs. the mythology of the West.

On the surface, much of Butcher’s Crossing reads like a “man vs. nature” tale. The buffalo hunt scenes are visceral, relentless, and shocking. Andrews watches the slaughter unfold, and it tears apart his belief in what he thought nature was, or what he needed it to be. At one point Williams writes:

“It came to him that he had sickened and turned away because of his shock at seeing the buffalo, a few moments before proud and noble and full of the dignity of life, now stark and helpless, a length of inert meat, divested of itself… In that murder he had felt the destruction of something within him, and he had not been able to face it.”

But Butcher’s Crossing isn’t all raw brutality. There is much beauty in Andrews' quiet reflections, in the recognition of nature not as a backdrop but as a character that is impartial, magnificent, and utterly indifferent. Williams renders the landscape in such exacting detail that it dwarfs the men both physically and spiritually.

The novel carries immense moral and existential weight. Andrews isn’t just grappling with cold and hunger, but with disillusionment. Williams dismantles the romanticized notions of the “rugged West.” Andrews seeks transcendence and revelation; what he finds is more ambiguous, more broken, but also more honest.

The pacing can test a reader’s patience with its long stretches of wilderness, snow, and silence. But that is its design: the grind, the waiting, the monotony, all pressing in with the weight of reality.

Readers should know: Butcher’s Crossing is not an easy or uplifting novel. Those expecting redemption, heroism, or triumph will leave unsettled. What Williams offers instead is a haunting meditation on illusion and reality, on how ideals shatter when confronted with the indifferent world.

Over time, the novel works its way under your skin. If you value books that unsettle as much as they enlighten, that strip away myth in search of something truer, Butcher’s Crossing is one to devour. It delivers deeply in atmosphere, in moral weight, and character, but it demands just as much from its reader. It’s a journey not only into wilderness, but into the self.

Title: Things in Nature Merely Grow
Author: Yiyun Li
My Review:
Things in Nature Merely Grow will absolutely crush you, but in the best possible way. Yiyun Li writes with a clarity that both comforts and unsettles: this is not consolation, it’s confrontation.

Reading this book is like being invited into the deepest corners of what it means to live when much of your world has already ended. Li’s insights into suicide are staggering—what it isn’t, what it is, and all the ways our language fails to capture it. And her reflections on parenthood? Heartbreaking, necessary. She teaches us that love doesn’t always protect, that understanding may be more important than loving in the way we expect, and that grief is not a process with a finish line.

Li doesn’t write this book about grief’s ending. She writes it about the ongoing presence of loss and how love, memory, and identity persist even when lives have been lost. She holds onto facts, gestures, and moments that aren’t just remembrances but assertions of what continues, that her children are, in some way, still with her.

If you pick this up expecting easy comfort, you won’t find it. But if you’re ready to be challenged, to feel deeply, to have your assumptions about life and death turned inside out, this is one of those rare books that will stay with you. Heavy, yes. Real. And in its honesty, strangely life-affirming.

Title: Letters to a Young Poet
Author: Rainer Maria Rilke
My Review:
“Be patient toward all that is unsolved in your heart and try to love the questions themselves…”

Rilke wrote these letters to a young military cadet named Franz Xaver Kappus, who was struggling with whether to pursue poetry or stay in his conventional career path. What’s beautiful is that Rilke doesn’t just give writing advice, he gives life advice. These letters feel like a hand extended across time, guiding you toward introspection, faith, love, and gratitude.

Reading Letters to a Young Poet was profoundly calming. It’s the kind of book you underline, re-read, and let change you. Rilke reminds us to find beauty in solitude, to seek depth in the ordinary, and to reset our worldview toward something gentler, more patient, and more grateful.

Though it’s written to an aspiring poet, this book is for anyone who needs a mental reset or a quiet companion in moments of doubt. Rilke’s words reach beyond the page and feel like they’re addressed to you directly, urging you to slow down, breathe, and trust the unfolding of your own life.

If you’ve ever felt restless, uncertain, or in need of clarity, let Rilke’s wisdom wash over you. This slim little book has the power to alter the way you carry yourself through the world.

Title: Lord of the Flies: The Graphic Novel (A Penguin Classics Hardcover)
Author: William Golding

Title: Exit Party
Author: Emily St. John Mandel
My Review:
The world is ending, and Emily St. John Mandel is inviting us to the party!!!

No one captures the beauty of ordinary moments on the brink of catastrophe like Mandel. The hush before the collapse, the shimmer of illusions breaking, the slow realization that history has already shifted under your feet.

I have a feeling Exit Party is going to be haunting, dazzling, and impossible to put down. Who else is ready for Mandel’s next masterpiece?

Title: The Wager: A Tale of Shipwreck, Mutiny and Murder
Author: David Grann

Title: Katabasis
Author: R.F. Kuang
My Review:
Hell is not fire and brimstone. Hell is not demons gnashing their teeth. Hell is picking up your most anticipated dark academia release of the year… and realizing you don’t actually love it.

That’s where Katabasis left me: not damned, not destroyed, but slightly disappointed. Kuang’s writing still has plenty of sharpness—her technical, sciencey, and philosophical asides gave me exactly the academic fix I was craving, and when she leans into that mode, the book sings. But somewhere around page 300, the descent faltered. The pacing dragged, the atmosphere thinned, and the promised hell started looking more like a dimly lit waiting room.

What stings most is how much potential the underworld had. The courts of hell should have been dazzlingly strange, grotesque, unique—trials that mirrored their own distinct qualities. Instead, many blended together, bland when they should have been infernal. Kuang seemed to lose steam in imagining what Alice and Peter might face down there.

Meanwhile, the romance stepped up to fill the void. Which is fine—love in hell has its appeal—but their relationship often felt weighed down by artificial conflict, manufactured mistrust, the kind of drama that exists more to keep pages turning than because it feels true.

So no, this wasn’t the triumphant dark descent I’d hoped to buy, shelve, and revisit forever. I’m glad I borrowed it, because I doubt I’ll be rereading it anytime soon. Still, if you’re hungry for a dark academia book with some sharp ideas (and don’t mind a few circles that drag on longer than they should), I’d still say it’s worth a visit.

Because hell isn’t other people—it’s realizing the book you waited for turned out to be just a 3.25/5 stars.

Title: Life, and Death, and Giants
Author: Ron Rindo
My Review:
Thank you to St. Martin's Press for providing this book for review via NetGalley.

Life, and Death, and Giants is a novel about faith and community that follows Gabriel Fisher, an extraordinary young man whose unusual size and talents deeply impact his family, neighbors, and strangers whose lives he touches.

The writing is smooth and accessible, with a diverse cast and multiple perspectives that add richness to the story. Seeing Gabriel through different lenses gave the novel emotional depth, and I especially appreciated the glimpse into Amish life.

Some plot points, however, felt a little unbelievable, and the focus on those around Gabriel left me wishing for a deeper look at his inner life. The story also leaned predictable at times, though Rindo’s storytelling kept me turning the pages.

Overall, this is an engaging read that many fans of general fiction will enjoy. While not groundbreaking, it offers warmth, readability, and a moving exploration of family and community. For me, it landed at 3.75 stars (rounded to 4/5).

Title: A Splintering
Author: Dur e Aziz Amna
My Review:
Thank you to NetGalley and Duckworth Books for the ARC in exchange for my honest review.

A Splintering gripped me from the very first page, and my fascination with Tara’s hunger for more than the world offered her carried me straight through to the end. I was especially absorbed by her frank, sharp voice and the steady development of her character arc. Her flaws, and the way she wrestles with ambition, motherhood, and class expectations, made her a complex and relatable protagonist I was deeply invested in.

The novel explores feminist themes in an organic, unforced way. It doesn’t shy away from asking hard questions about what women owe their families, their children, themselves, and whether it is ever truly possible to “have it all.”

I highly recommend A Splintering to readers who enjoy literary fiction that delves into the messy complexities of ambition, motherhood, and identity.

4.25/5

Title: Now Is Not the Time to Panic
Author: Kevin    Wilson
My Review:
4.25⭐️

Kevin Wilson’s Now Is Not the Time to Panic proves once again why he’s the master of taking an absurd premise and spinning it into gold. His off-the-wall humor is sharp as ever, and his characters are vivid, quirky, and unforgettable.

The setup is deceptively simple: two teenagers pull a silly stunt that spirals far beyond what they ever imagined. From there, Wilson unpacks not just the chaos of adolescence, but also the weight of creativity, identity, and consequences. He nails that feeling of being a teenager—the restlessness, the intensity, the strange mix of fear and freedom—and somehow makes it both nostalgic and raw.

What I love most is the balance: the book is playful and lighthearted on the surface, but beneath it Wilson weaves in heavier themes that hit harder here than in the other two of his books I’ve read. It’s a feel-good novel that doesn’t shy away from complexity, all while never taking itself too seriously.

If you like stories that start with the absurd and end with something deeply human, this one’s a gem.

Title: Hurricane Season
Author: Fernanda Melchor
My Review:
DAMN. This was an experience. Brutal, visceral, and unrelenting. Melchor’s prose is staggering!

The novel paints a town that feels cursed, a case study of so many things like poverty, violence, drugs, gender, sexuality, hopelessness/futility, all swirling together in a relentless storm. (you see what I did there? 😜)

This is what I would call a low enjoyment, high appreciation read-- I’m thrilled to have discovered Melchor and will 100% read more of her work, but while Hurricane Season was unforgettable, it was also exhausting, claustrophobic, and anxiety-inducing.

I’M TORN on what to rate this! Based on enjoyment, it’s a 3. Based on craft, it feels like a 4 (or even higher?!). Let’s call it a solid 3.5⭐️.

Recommended to readers ready for a brutal, demanding experience. This is a book that will stick with you, but it asks a lot in return. Before you read don't forget to check the TWs!

Title: The Goldfinch
Author: Donna Tartt
My Review:
The Goldfinch is undeniably ambitious. Tartt has the chops to tackle a story sprawling across decades, cities, and themes. But did it all come together in a satisfying way?

The book’s strengths lie mainly in its exploration of fate, beauty, and the randomness of existence. Structurally, it’s impressive. The story is woven with echoes and returns that tie the ending neatly back to the beginning, giving the novel a satisfying circularity even if the journey meanders. Her prose is solid and functional but infrequently dazzling.

The first misstep? Theo himself. He felt bland, hard to connect with, and often too passive—smothered by circumstance. Hobie and Pippa were a delight, but instead of more of them we got more Boris. Yes, Boris was entertaining at times—funny, over the top, a sharp contrast to Theo—but whole stretches with him, plus plotlines like Kitzy, the endless drug binges, and the mafia-ish Amsterdam detour, felt superfluous. The book dragged even when things were “happening.” With tighter editing, it could have easily been under 500 pages.

Ironically, the novel’s looseness, which framed the story in a way that gave it massive potential, ended up being one of its biggest issues. Its large scope ultimately makes it easy to get lost or disconnected. Unlike The Secret History, the focus here often felt diffuse, and I never felt fully gripped.

The bottom line: The Goldfinch is memorable but not life-changing. At 700+ pages, I wanted to be swept away, but I mostly trudged through.

Would I recommend it? Maybe, to Tartt fans and die-hard literary fiction readers. To the average reader? Probably not, because my final verdict is that this is a challenging and bloated novel that may feel “not worth it” to many readers.

3.25⭐️

Title: Narrow the Road
Author: James   Wade
My Review:
Narrow the Road is a mix of western adventure and Southern Gothic. The narrative follows a protagonist searching for his father.

The prose is solid and consistently elevates the story. The novel tackles heavier themes like loss and morality without coming off as preachy, while the humor lands well and provides much-needed comic relief.

This isn’t quite a can’t-put-it-down read, but that’s actually a strength. It unfolds at a steady pace and is never boring. Each encounter on the journey brings fully realized characters, each with a distinct, authentic voice. Wade has a remarkable knack for fleshing out characters so they feel real and memorable.

Overall, this is one of the best 2025 releases I’ve read so far. I’d recommend it to anyone who enjoys westerns or Southern Gothic, especially readers drawn to character-driven storytelling over plot-driven suspense.

Title: Run for the Hills
Author: Kevin    Wilson
My Review:
A quirky, heartwarming road trip full of laughs and feels.

Kevin Wilson has a gift for mixing sharp humor with genuine heart. The premise is absurd, (siblings tracking down the trail of a dad who kept reinventing himself) but it becomes a surprisingly tender story about family, identity, and connection.

I laughed out loud at the zany situations and rooted for these characters as they figured out what it means to belong. It’s a true feel-good novel without being overly saccharine.

Recommended for fans of Fredrik Backman (A Man Called Ove, Beartown). If you like funny, big-hearted stories that leave you smiling, you’ll probably love this too!

Title: Atmosphere
Author: Taylor Jenkins Reid
My Review:
3.75 ⭐

Let’s start with the title: Atmosphere. At first it struck me as vague, maybe even lazy. But the more I thought about it, the more it clicked. The title seems to work on two levels—the literal atmosphere an astronaut must break through, and the metaphorical atmosphere of fear, shame, and societal pressure the protagonist feels trapped in. Just as she must conquer her fear of space and risk her life, she must also risk everything to embrace love. That parallel gave the title more meaning for me.

Now, to the big question: Is this as good as The Seven Husbands of Evelyn Hugo or Daisy Jones & The Six? For me, not quite. While there are some tense space-set moments, don’t expect a nonstop thrill ride. The real heart of the novel is in Reid’s character work, which is mostly excellent. Most of the main cast feels layered and real, though one slipped into caricature, and a couple of side characters were forgettable.

The 1980s setting works perfectly for exploring a “forbidden” romance, though the circumstances behind that romance stretched believability at times. Still, the emotional stakes carried the story.

In the end, Atmosphere delivers an engaging, character-driven story with flashes of Reid’s brilliance, even if it doesn’t soar to the heights of her best work.

Title: The Neon Bible
Author: John Kennedy Toole
My Review:
4.5 ⭐

John Kennedy Toole once dismissed The Neon Bible as a “bad book.” I have to strongly disagree. Yes, it's not perfect and he wrote it at sixteen, but what struck me is just how good it actually is—an engrossing, atmospheric, and surprisingly mature exploration of small-town life in the American South.

Through the voice of young David, Toole creates a vivid, realistic portrait of growing up under the weight of poverty, religion, and societal judgment. David’s narration feels raw, authentic, and deeply human. At times it is tender and at other times heartbreaking.

What’s most fascinating is how much promise this novel shows. You can see in these pages the early sparks of the literary genius who would later give us A Confederacy of Dunces.

This is an absolute must-read for fans of Toole or of Southern Gothic literature in general.

Title: We Are Always Tender With Our Dead (Burnt Sparrow, #1)
Author: Eric LaRocca
My Review:
I knew going into We Are Always Tender With Our Dead that LaRocca has a reputation for pushing boundaries, and this book is no exception. This first entry in the Burnt Sparrow trilogy is unsettling, visceral, and deeply disturbing. Horror fans looking for a bleak and nightmarish read will find much to appreciate here.

LaRocca’s artistry shows in his vivid depictions of violence. The graphic descriptions are purposefully tied to themes like the brutality of humanity, the darkness of human nature, the corrosive power of shame, and the prejudice and bigotry that fester in small communities. The worldbuilding is strong, dropping readers straight into a grim, claustrophobic landscape that feels both immersive and relentless.

That said, there were a few aspects that didn’t entirely work for me. One choice that broke my trust as a reader was the inclusion of a story told by a character, which felt shoehorned in and came across as filler or a repurposed short story. It pulled me out of the narrative. At times, I also questioned the authenticity of character relationships, since their dynamics felt either flat or overly forced. Lastly, while I can forgive some ambiguity in the first book of a trilogy, I do wish LaRocca had rewarded me with a bit more insight into why events unfolded as they did.

Overall, the book delivered on bleak atmosphere, disturbing imagery, and striking ideas, but its uneven execution didn’t quite achieve a lingering chill or spark the desire for me to continue with the series.

Rating: ⭐⭐½ (Rounded up)

Title: The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas
Author: Machado de Assis
Additional Authors: Enylton de Sá Rego, Gilberto Pinheiro Passos, Gregory Rabassa
My Review:
A dead underachiever justifying his pathetic life? Right up my alley.

Machado de Assis was so ahead of his time that this 1881 novel, written in the age of literary realism, reads as if it were modern or even postmodern. His bold, groundbreaking style brims with playful irony and formal experimentation, gleefully breaking with tradition. The story isn’t linear; it jumps, digresses, mocks itself, and even interrupts the reader.

This should be required reading for anyone who loves the classics and wants to see the roots of later experimental fiction. I loved its themes: the liberation of death, the futility of ambition, the absurdity of life. At a time when most literature exalted heroes and great deeds, Assis dared to give us the anti-heroic memoir of a man who accomplished nothing.

And the cherry on top? After narrating his countless failings, Brás Cubas claims one great victory, but I won’t spoil it. You’ll have to read this strange, brilliant masterpiece to find out.

My Review:
Madonna in a Fur Coat is one of those novels where the beauty lies as much in the prose as in the story it tells. The writing has a quiet elegance to it.

The relationship at the heart of the book is by turns strange, frustrating, and moving. As the worlds of two flawed people collide, the story reveals how the messiness of love often mirrors the messiness of life itself. It reads like a case study in how communication, silence, and mismatched expectations can shape intimacy.

I came away impressed by how alive the characters felt, and I understand why this novel has endured and earned its reputation as a modern classic. I’d recommend it to readers looking for a literary and contemplative take on romance. It's less about sweeping passion, and more about the small, complicated truths of being human.

My Review:
3.5 rounded up

Heartwood was an above-average read for me. Gaige’s exploration of multiple POVs kept the story engaging and each voice felt distinct and added freshness and depth to the narrative. The characters are diverse and likable, with interesting backstories.

I appreciated that the novel is much more than just a straightforward missing-person mystery. Gaige uses the search for Sparrow as a thread to connect the side characters’ lives in an exploration of circumstance, relationships, and personal struggles.

That said, readers looking for a raw, gritty thriller might find this too gentle. It leans more toward light mystery blended with literary fiction. While it never reached a “mind-blowing” level for me, Heartwood was consistently pleasant and interesting enough to keep me turning the pages.

A thoughtful, character-driven story that’s more about connection than suspense.

Title: The Passion According to G.H.
Author: Clarice Lispector
My Review:
3.5⭐️

The Passion According to G.H. definitely feels like it is in the same vein as Agua Viva, but it hits quite differently. The Passion convinced me that Lispector really is on another level when it comes to seeing and understanding the world and existence.

While many of her philosophical musings went over my head, they were still fascinating to sit with. I didn’t like this as much as Hour of the Star, but it’s a close second. When reading The Passion, you get the sense that even if Lispector didn’t fully know what she was talking about, it’s clear she had at least convinced herself that she did.

Honestly, it’s pretty darn impressive how much philosophy she managed to eke out of an encounter with a cockroach.

Title: A Confederacy of Dunces
Author: John Kennedy Toole
My Review:
This is easily one of the funniest books I’ve ever read. Toole’s New Orleans bursts with absurdity, and Ignatius J. Reilly might be one of the most unforgettable protagonists in literature. He’s infuriating, grotesque, ridiculous, yet strangely magnetic.

What I loved is that beyond the comedy, the novel has real weight. Its satire digs into society, work, art, and human foolishness in ways that make you think long after the laughter fades. At times the pacing drags and a few characters could have been more developed, but honestly, those flaws barely matter compared to the sheer enjoyment of reading it.

It’s the kind of book you can flip open to any page and instantly be entertained. A perfectly imperfect masterpiece that I love.

Title: Questions About Angels
Author: Billy Collins
My Review: Questions About Angels by Billy Collins was such a pleasant surprise. This was my first time reading him, and I was instantly drawn in by how approachable his poetry feels. His work is relatable, funny, and clever in a way that makes you want to keep turning the pages. The simplicity of his style makes the poems easy to read, but there’s always a spark of wit or a moment of reflection that lingers. The variety of topics kept the collection fresh and engaging from start to finish. Overall, a delightful and rewarding read.

Title: Água Viva
Author: Clarice Lispector
My Review:
2.75⭐️

Água Viva isn’t a novel in the traditional sense, and I think that’s important to know before picking it up. Lispector has created something much more experimental: a lyrical, stream-of-consciousness work that reads like a long prose poem or philosophical diary. Spoiler alert: there’s no plot, no characters to follow, just a narrator drifting through thoughts on time, sensation, art, and existence.

So, if you go in expecting a story, you’ll probably be disappointed. But if you enjoy untethered philosophical musings, you might find a lot to appreciate here!

For me, the musings felt a bit too meandering and broad in scope, without much focus to anchor me. Maybe I wasn’t in the right state of mind for it because I found myself craving something more structured. On the flip side, this same sweeping, unrestrained quality could be exactly what another reader is looking for, especially if they’re in the mood to let their mind wander along with the narrator.

The writing itself is beautiful, which is no surprise coming from Lispector. Her sentences often stop you in your tracks. Even though Água Viva didn’t resonate with me as much as The Hour of the Star, I still admire the talent and originality behind it.

My Review:
★★★★★

This book CONSUMED me.

The Passion is romantic, tragic, addicting, weird, funny, and unexpectedly profound. I was swept away by the alternating perspectives of Henri and Villanelle, which were both unforgettable in their own way, and by the way their stories twist together against the backdrop of war, love, and fate.

Winterson’s prose is absolutely stunning: sometimes a single word hits like a dart, other times a long, winding sentence builds into something equally sharp and devastating. She blends humor, heartbreak, and surreal touches so seamlessly that I often had to pause just to take it in.

This novel came out of nowhere for me and has instantly joined my list of all-time favorites. I can’t recommend it enough, especially if you want a story that will pull you under and refuse to let go.

Title: The Hour of the Star
Author: Clarice Lispector
My Review:
Lispector’s The Hour of the Star is brief, strange, and brimming with philosophical bite. The fractured grammar and spiraling syntax feel jarring at first, but gradually reveal a deliberate rhythm. It’s less a story than an existential dissection, full of contrasts like poverty and detachment, innocence and cruelty, beauty and ugliness.

Not an instant favorite, but the kind of book that lingers and will likely reward rereading.

3.5⭐️

Title: Flush
Author: Virginia Woolf
My Review:
Flush is an unexpected delight! It’s witty, touching, and quietly profound.

Virginia Woolf takes the life of Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s cocker spaniel and turns it into a rich, layered narrative that’s part biography, part social commentary, and part canine memoir.

Flush isn’t just a charming literary dog; he’s a fully developed character whose emotions, instincts, and perceptions shift over time in ways that feel both true to animal nature and deeply human. Watching him grow from a small pup to an older dog was immensely satisfying.

Woolf’s prose is as luminous and precise as ever. Her ability to inhabit the mind of a dog while subtly observing class, culture, and gender makes this much more than a “dog book.” And yet, it is also an incredibly fun, tender story. You can read it purely for the joy of the narrative.

Highly recommended for Woolf fans, dog lovers, and anyone who enjoys seeing the world through unexpected eyes.

Title: Victorian Psycho
Author: Virginia Feito
My Review:
Victorian Psycho is entertaining, weird and disturbingly humorous. The novel’s violence is simultaneously unsettling and fun.

The novelty wore off a bit around the 75% mark, but it’s still an easy, fast-paced read that horror fans or lovers of dark humor will likely enjoy.

Not a new favorite, but I’m glad I read it!

Title: Human Acts
Author: Han Kang
My Review:
2.25 ⭐️ // Respectfully not for me

Human Acts is one of those books that I respect more than I enjoyed. Han Kang’s political bravery in writing about the Gwangju Uprising is undeniable. The way she mixes fiction, nonfiction, philosophy, and even ghost story elements is bold, and most likely the reason this novel resonates deeply with many readers. But personally? I found it emotionally exhausting, repetitive, and bleak in a way that left little room to breathe.

The prose is restrained, probably intentionally so, to mirror themes of censorship and collective numbness. Covering grief, violence, and trauma from many different angles makes for a monotonous and draining reading experience. I never really connected with the characters, perhaps because the structure kept resetting before I could get invested.

I would likely only recommend Human Acts to someone with a strong interest in South Korean political history or in literary explorations of national trauma. Otherwise, I’d probably steer readers toward books that explore grief or violence with a bit more nuance, lyricism, or emotional variety.

Title: Notes on Infinity
Author: Austin   Taylor
My Review:
⭐️⭐️⭐️💫 (3.25 stars)

Notes on Infinity follows Harvard students Zoe and Jack as they discover what may be a cure for aging and launch a secret biotech startup, Manna, that catapults them into fame, fortune, and eventually, scandal. It’s a compelling premise, one that instantly reminded me of Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow: college-age protagonists, intellectual sparks, and a shared creative venture. But, where Gabrielle Zevin’s novel dug deep into themes of friendship, mortality, and meaning, this one felt more surface-level.

The writing is straightforward and accessible, with a steady, fast-paced flow that kept me engaged (I finished the audiobook in two days). There’s not much in the way of lush description or voice-y prose. It reads more like a clean, commercially-oriented narrative than something literary or stylized. Zoe’s voice didn’t stand out to me as particularly unique or vivid, and the characters overall felt more like archetypes than fully developed people. This lack of depth made the emotional stakes feel a bit muted.

Themes like immortality and ambition are present, but Taylor barely grazes the surface of infinity or the existential weight of curing aging, which seemed like a missed opportunity. The novel instead focuses on the business side of the startup. That angle will appeal to readers interested in tech drama and ambition, but I personally wanted more exploration of personal stakes, character interiority, and moral complexity.

What I’ll remember most is how much potential the book had in its premise. I kept waiting for it to dig deeper, to surprise me, to break out of its clean structure, but it stayed on a safe, familiar path. Still, it was entertaining and never dull, just not as emotionally or thematically rich as I hoped.

If you're looking for a quick, engaging read with a tech-savvy plot and light drama, Notes on Infinity delivers. If you're hoping for literary depth or memorable characters, this might feel more like a sketch than a masterpiece.
