Title: Wonder
Author: Chris Emery
My Review:
In "Wonder", Chris Emery explores awe, beauty, history, and the marvels of everyday life.

He leans heavily into vivid imagery, obscure word choices, and surprising juxtapositions, aiming to offer fresh perspectives. While I appreciated the intent, the execution didn’t quite land for me. Much of the "wonder" I experienced was me wondering if I was missing something, or if the meaning just wasn’t there.

I kept waiting for a poem to truly stick with me, but instead of awe, I mostly felt mild puzzlement or indifference.

Though some pieces felt playful, Emery largely avoids rhyme, rhythm, or sound play like alliteration. Several free verse poems didn’t feel especially poetic, and the meter was sometimes clunky enough to trip over.

That said, I respect the effort to capture fleeting, intimate moments and to move between the mundane and fantastical. The collection has a distinct aesthetic, but it didn’t leave much of an impression on me. If you enjoy experimental imagery and don’t mind a lack of lyrical flow or emotional weight, this may work better for you. For me, it was an uneven read that never quite found its footing.

2.5/5 Rounded up.

Title: The Vegetarian
Author: Han Kang
My Review:
3.25 ⭐️

When I first heard the premise of The Vegetarian, I thought, “Okay, that sounds… a little gimmicky?” Like, how dramatic can someone going vegetarian really be? Turns out: VERY.

This book isn’t about tofu, folks. It’s about control, autonomy, and trying to escape the world’s cruelty.

The plot? Honestly unbelievable, but also kind of riveting. There were multiple times I sat there thinking “Wait… what??” but also couldn’t stop reading. The outrageousness of it all veers into darkly comic territory for me, even though the themes are anything but light.

Yeong-hye’s alienation hit home for me. I mean, haven’t we all wanted to tap out of this world’s nonsense at some point?

That said, some parts didn’t fully work for me. The “vegetarianism as radical rebellion” angle still feels a bit much at times.

If you like quietly unhinged books, character studies with heavy themes, and don’t mind a plot that’s a bit out there, then yes. Go in with an open mind, and maybe an empty stomach.

Title: Bees, and After (Volume 119) (Yale Series of Younger Poets)
Author: John Liles
My Review:
Is "jargon poetry" a thing? If not, "Bees, and After" might be the first entry of a new genre that could easily be called that, or even "science-core".

It’s not the easiest read, but certainly a unique one.

This collection occupies a curious space where science meets art. John Liles experiments with form, often presenting poems in creative typographic layouts that visually echo the complexity of the subject matter.

Liles explores scientific phenomena through fragmented, lyrical, and frequently enigmatic verse. At times, reading it feels like browsing through a series of poeticized science lecture notes. While the poems rarely rhyme, there’s a rhythmic quality to the language that carries the reader through, as long as they don't get bogged down by trying to decipher the abundant technical terminology.

Luckily, Liles had the foresight to helpfully include footnotes for many of these terms. But, eventually, I stopped trying to analyze every scientific detail and instead read continuously, letting the rhythm and imagery wash over me.

Some topics hit close to home, like the heart beginning and ceasing to beat, or the fact that it’s the first organ to form and function. Others are wonderfully obscure, like a meditation on the most abundant mineral in the earth’s mantle.

Ultimately, some of these poems work beautifully and others less so. "Bees, and After" is not a book to breeze through, but for those willing to engage with it fully, it offers a thoughtful experience.

My Review:
Han Kang’s prose is stunning, immersive, and at times hypnotic. The imagery in We Do Not Part often stopped me in my tracks with its beauty.

That said, this book just wasn’t for me because its positive aspects were dragged down by the heaviness of the content, which is steeped in war violence, trauma, and the lingering psychological aftermath of conflict.

While Kang explores these themes in a deeply creative way, I often found myself feeling distanced rather than engaged. The violence was emotionally exhausting.

I admire this novel for its ambition and artistry, but the subject matter and emotional tone left me cold. A beautifully written book that I can’t say I enjoyed.

Title: The Left Hand of Darkness
Author: Ursula K. Le Guin
My Review:
I really wanted to love this classic since I know how bold and groundbreaking Le Guin’s exploration of gender and sexual identity was in 1969!

Not only that, but Le Guin prioritized character and cultural development at a time when science fiction was largely plot-driven.

That said… I found the book pretty boring.

Much of the political intrigue and worldbuilding went over my head. I got tangled in the dense terminology and the unfamiliar fictional nations/ethnicities. The plot didn’t feel particularly high-stakes, and the dynamic between two protagonists was supposed to carry emotional weight, but it just didn’t land for me.

I respect what Le Guin achieved here, but ultimately this book was more of an intellectual experience than an enjoyable one for me.

Title: Death Comes for the Archbishop
Author: Willa Cather
My Review:
I went into Death Comes for the Archbishop not knowing what to expect—the title felt dramatic, but the story is anything but. It’s a slow-paced, reflective, and quietly emotional novel about a life of service and faith in the American Southwest.

Cather follows Father Jean Marie Latour as he arrives in New Mexico in 1851 to serve as Apostolic Vicar. Over nearly forty years, he navigates a vast, unforgiving landscape shaped by Mexican and Indigenous traditions, spreading his faith gently and persistently.

Rather than focusing on conflict, the novel offers a meditative portrait of a changing region and a man shaped by it. It reminded me of Lonesome Dove in its attention to the frontier, though this story centers more on spirituality than adventure. Thoughtful and beautifully written, it’s a classic worth reading.

My Review:
4.25

The most horrific non-horror novel I’ve ever read. It’s impossible to discuss Fox without mentioning Lolita or My Dark Vanessa. Oates seems determined to go even further, and she does. She plunges disturbingly deep into the minds of predator and victim alike. Even the bystanders get psychological depth, which sometimes makes the book feel overlong, but the writing is so sharp it’s hard to complain.

Fox is unsettling, intimate, and painfully human. You finish it feeling complicit, like you’ve witnessed something you were never meant to see. It would be hard to deny that Fox is as brilliant as it is haunting.

Author: Italo Calvino
My Review:
Calvino’s prose is undeniably beautiful! And the premise is brilliant: Marco Polo describes fantastical cities to Kublai Khan.
Unfortunately, the unconventional narrative structure here was something more to appreciate than to enjoy.

I found it hard to stay engaged, as it eventually felt like reliving the same dream over and over, with only small details shifting. The “is it real or imagined?” angle wore thin for me. Overall, it was still a fascinating book I might revisit someday, but not soon.

My Review: Ocean Vuong’s prose is as sharp and lyrical as ever, and the humor unexpectedly shines. Some characters are deeply memorable. But the emotional depth felt forced, and certain themes came across more like boxes to check than truths to uncover. A well-written book that didn’t fully land for me. 3.25 ⭐️

Title: The Lowlife
Author: Alexander Baron
My Review:
I’m genuinely surprised The Lowlife isn’t more widely read!

This unexpectedly delightful novel tells a seemingly simple story that holds a lot of depth beneath the surface. Harryboy Boas, a gambler and self-described lowlife drifts through London, and his interactions with a neighboring family reveal a quiet, aching portrait of adulthood, loneliness, and the ways people seek connection.

Baron portrays characters living lives of quiet desperation with empathy and clarity, weaving a good amount of humor into the story, even as it deals with heavier themes.

Baron’s writing is sharp, the dialogue rings true, and the emotional undercurrents feel lived-in rather than forced. It’s a thoughtful, funny, and ultimately very human novel. I’d recommend it to anyone interested in under-the-radar literary fiction that balances grit with grace.

Title: If on a Winter's Night a Traveller
Author: Italo Calvino
My Review:
If it isn’t clear from its sentence fragment title, If on a winter’s night a traveller is metafiction. In fact, from the very beginning Calvino breaks the fourth wall, using a title that seems to speak directly to the reader: “You’ve never heard of a novel called something like this… isn’t it intriguing? Go ahead, pick up this book and read it.” And few readers will be disappointed by the promise of a story as strange as its title, because this one truly is delightfully weird, in all the best ways.

From the moment the novel opens in the second person, the reader should know that this will be anything but a conventional story. The narrative alternates between your quest to read a novel and the first chapters of ten different books. At times, it feels a little disorienting, like being dropped into a literary funhouse, but mostly curiosity consistently pulls you forward along a surprisingly joyful journey.

Much of the novel’s charm lies in Calvino’s openness about what he’s doing, how he’s doing it, and why. You might expect that kind of self-awareness to cheapen the literary effect, but instead, he sidesteps gimmickry altogether by breaking the rules (or more accurately, rewriting them) as he goes.

The result is a story so unpredictable, so alive with invention, that it’s impossible to look away. You keep reading because you don’t want to miss whatever breathtaking, playful, or profound turn it will take next.

This one is definitely for those who love books about books, or stories that invite you to be part of the game.

While marketed as horror, I found the atmosphere and violence more repetitive than frightening. The brutality felt flat and like it lacked stakes, making it hard to stay emotionally invested. I found my attention drifting and it was hard to stay engaged which caused scenes to blur together, and I struggled to understand the purpose behind much of the journey, or the bond between the main characters. I never found the deep character development or emotional tension I was waiting for.

Overall, this book simply wasn’t for me. I went in hoping for a haunting, character-driven story during a terrifying period in history, and came away feeling mostly unmoved. But, if you’re a fan of dark historical fantasy with apocalyptic religious themes, it might strike differently.

Title: The Phoenix Pencil Company

My Review:
Thank you to NetGalley, William Morrow, and Allison King for the opportunity to read and review this ARC.

The Phoenix Pencil Company is an ambitious blend of the genres of fantasy, historical fiction, and contemporary adult fiction. Not only does King do a commendable job of bridging these genres, but she also weaves together an array of themes, including memory, storytelling, data sharing, and familial legacy.

The magical concept of "reforging" may be a hurdle for some readers-- regular fantasy consumers are likely to be more receptive to this inherited ability that is central to the narrative, while others might find it gimmicky. Despite the lack of a detailed origin story, King uses reforging effectively as a device to explore communication during war and across generations.

In contrast to the unfamiliarity of reforging, the EMBRs software platform, which aggregates user data into comprehensive personal narratives, will feel all too familiar. Most readers are already engaged in the ongoing fight for data privacy, making this subplot feel somewhat predictable, if not a little boring.

At its heart, The Phoenix Pencil Company is about relationships, and King writes them in a tender and relatable way-- whether it’s the unfolding of first love or the dynamic between grandparents and grandchild.

The novel’s journal entry/epistolary format makes sense within the context of the story, but its execution sometimes falls short, leading to moments of awkwardness. Fortunately, these issues aren't significant enough to detract from the novel’s strengths.

Title: The Great Gatsby
Author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
My Review:
The Great Gatsby was not a hit when it was published in 1925. Wait, what?! The beloved classic that everyone and their mother's dog has read hasn't always been considered the peak of American literature?

Well, first impressions aren't always right, but, in the case of a novel like The Great Gatsby, you can't help but ask why it wasn't immediately hailed as a masterpiece.

Here are my takes:

First off, you rarely (if ever) hear anyone talk about its protagonist, Nick Carraway-- and why would they? He's bland, boring, passive. The best he can do is sit back and make vaguely “deep” observations that come off like little more than an attempt to sound wise.

Next, at under 200 pages, the book is too short. Fitzgerald attempted to tackle the themes of wealth, the American Dream, class divisions, consumerism, and more, but he just barely scratched the surface because he needed more pages to fully flesh out the points he was trying to make. So, this novel comes of as half (or less) baked.

These issues aside, Fitzgerald's prose is solid. And it's hard not to respect a story that can garner so many fans when its plot is so unapologetically tragic. The Great Gatsby's characters may not be the most likeable, but their flaws make them human in a way that it seems like the vast majority of readers and relate to.

Overall, the mixed reviews The Great Gatsby originally received feel more like an honest representation of how good the novel is than all the 5-star reviews posted online nowadays.

3.25⭐️

Title: Source Code: My Beginnings
Author: Bill  Gates
My Review: 2.25⭐️ As a huge Bill Gates fan I had high hopes that Source Code: My Beginnings would be a great book that I could recommend to others. Unfortunately, I was a bit let down— it’s not a bad book, but it turned out to be one that I might reply “meh” to when asked how it is. While it is enjoyable to read about Gates childhood, coming of age, and how he found his footing in the nascent PC industry, by the 3/4 mark the story gets bogged down by extraneous details that make it hard to stay engaged. Not only that, but this book also suffers from its limited scope— it would be a more well-rounded read if it did a better job of tying the story back to modern day and offered more insight on how Gates’ source code continues to be a foundational part of how he operates.

Title: Invisible Man
Author: Ralph Ellison
My Review:
Readers who go in blind will likely not be prepared for Invisible Man.

Heck, even those acquainted with novels in the same vein may not be ready for Ellison's strain of experimental literary jazz.

Invisible Man’s stream of consciousness is a powerful wave that crashes over the reader—an opportunity to bask in the rawness of Ellison’s message and the feeling it creates.

The unique and passionate voices of Ellison’s characters are always front and center. They magnify—and are magnified by—his masterful command of prose, imagery, and characterization.

Like a niche subgenre of jazz, Invisible Man’s quirks, dissonances, and surrealism may put off some readers—but those who make it to the last page will likely return to it again, noticing a bassline here, a new harmony there, that they didn’t hear before.

My Review: Dracula's reputation precedes it, and that's a big problem.  Luckily, the novel at least manages to deliver on spooky atmosphere-- it's no surprise that this was a groundbreaking and shocking novel when it was published over a century ago, with it's violent and paranormal content.  Unfortunately, these details don't hit that hard when you take the novel as a whole because they are overshadowed by many drawn-out passages that leave the reader yawning and wondering when they will reach the next exciting scene.  I may not read Dracula again anytime soon, but the next time I do I will likely reach for an abridged version.

My Review:
Read on a whim, I was shocked to find out that this wasn't a debut novel, but I guess there's a good reason they named failed 2nd efforts "sophomore slumps".

While it is a big surprise that this novel was nominated for a couple of awards, it's hardly shocking that it didn't actually win any. Real Americans sounds good on the surface, but if the blurb were to give away it's gimmicky plot and theme I suspect that no one would read it. The promised "immersive, moving prose" is blatantly absent and the only thing "profound" about it was my profound urge to DNF the novel from the start of part 2 all the way until the end. (I persisted out of spite)

I wish someone had told me how bad this was and not to read it, so I am doing everyone a courtesy and letting them know that this is a waste of your time.

My Review:
Let's balance out all those 5 star reviews a little bit-- Homegoing is overrated for what it is.

That's not to say that there aren't some interesting narrative threads, but it feels like some get lost, some don't belong, and those that remain struggle to form themselves into a cohesive tapestry.

Unfortunately, this leads one to conclude that Gyasi was overambitious-- there is too much going on here, too many characters, too many years covered. At it's core, Homegoing contains wonderful themes and messages, but they are detracted from by an attempt to write the next great epic, in which the execution is lacking.

Title: The Book of Disquiet
Author: Fernando Pessoa
My Review: A tough book to read makes a tough book to review.  Pessoa’s “The Book Of Disquiet” is repetitive and self indulgent, but should we expect much different from what is basically a collection of diary-like entries that explore the psyche of the writer from every possible angle? Even if we don’t hold The B. Of D. to the standard of novels (because it isn’t one) it’s still a bit disappointing because there are moments of genius that ignite with a glorious blaze, only to be snuffed out seconds later by the tiresome ramblings that rehash territory that was already covered. No doubt, Pessoa’s dedication to working on The B. of D. over the course of decades is impressive, but it’s also unfortunate because any work that goes on that long is bound to have continuity issues, plus a need for a God-like editor.  Unsurprisingly, The Book reads essentially like an authentically unedited journal, one by a writer that showed little-to-no restraint because he was still in the drafting stage. That just means that The B. of D. falls very short of reaching its full potential, and it’s too bad Pessoa wasn’t able to complete this work, because I suspect he would be just as unhappy with its current state as I am.

My Review: 3.25. The two narratives that make up  Playground are quite distinct, and it’s really a roll of the dice for which one the reader will connect with more. While there is plenty to admire about the risk of entangling these two contrasting storylines, in the case that one doesn’t resonate, Power’s story relies on the grace and hope of the reader that things will eventually “click” in a way that makes it worth it.  Unfortunately, for this reader, and I suspect for many others, the eventual merging of the stories is less like fireworks and more like a misfire.  If the reader connects with both sides of the Playground coin, great, but if not, they will likely feel cheated, especially if one half of the novel boils down the passionate, carried away ramblings of an author and his failed attempt to insert them in a way that makes sense.

Title: Intermezzo
Author: Sally Rooney
My Review:
The beautiful chessboard on Intermezzo's cover shows shadows of people, hinting that the novel explores relationships-- a suggestion that Rooney abundantly fulfills. However, problems could start if the reader internalizes the image on the cover of the book too much, maybe anticipating some of the sexy drama and strategy that typically go into a game of chess.

Even if the cover isn't meant to be taken literally, one might imagine that, since the title suggests that the story explores something akin to an intervening or interruptive period or event, that the characters (as shown in the cover art) are in various positions on the board, in a half-played-out state. Now that the stage is set, where will they go next, what will they do?

While the answer is "not much"-- they may ruminate, they may aimlessly wander around a plane of black and white squares-- that's ok, because there are plenty of spans in a game of chess where it feels like not a lot happens, or it's hard to follow what its going on. Plus, it's possible to appreciate the movements of the pieces for their own sake, as they dance around the board. Rooney has managed to capture the sense that we are following people who are doing the same thing that we are, focusing on the present moment and living our lives in the only way we know how.

So, what if Rooney is tongue-in-cheekly trying to convey that life and chess, both complicated as they are, are actually nothing like each other? The likely response from Rooney die-hards: "don't judge the book by its cover." Understandable-- with Intermezzo, Rooney is just doing more of what she has done successfully in her past novels, blending all the the likely ingredients of literary fiction and the human condition (grief, romance, mental health) into an interesting scenario.

Title: A Little Life
Author: Hanya Yanagihara
My Review:
You've heard it's "torture porn"-- but with all these 5 star reviews...it must be an exaggeration...how bad can it be, really? Plus, you love literary fiction.

After reading some more reviews, you're hesitant. But, there are still SO MANY 5 star reviews...what if this has the potential to be one of your favorite reads?

You just have to know.

You start reading. Hmm, this isn't bad so far. Yikes, I'm starting to see a bit of what they were referring to, but there are still some really beautiful moments.

The beautiful moments have started to be overshadowed by the pain. Ugh, this is getting brutal, really brutal.

Wow, pain pain pain. This is actually difficult to listen to, the honesty, the gratuitous suffering and torment. The end can't come soon enough.

You plow through the pain, the torture, the agony. You emerge at the other end feeling like Frodo after he finally threw the ring into Mt. Doom to destroy it.

But you don't feel joy or satisfaction, only regret.

But at least you know.

Title: The Maniac
Author: Benjamín Labatut
My Review:
Never before has the narrative surrounding artificial intelligence- its origins, development, and implications for the future- been more relevant.

Labatut’s exploration of this topic in The MANIAC is laid out, appropriately, like the three parts of a game of go (or chess)— key players and seeds of ideas are set up in the opening, then the the reader enters the meat of the middlegame with a deep dive into John Von Neumann’s obsession with the mathematical precursors to AI, and, finally, the unforgettable and all-important endgame is reached with the extension and application of those ideas that had been spawned in fits of mania over seventy years prior.

The result is a captivating micro and macro view of Von Neumann that showcases not only the diverse viewpoints of those close to him but also the path of the waves he made that tore through the world so many years ago-- ones that we still feel the ripples of to this very day.

He does a great job at keeping the reader interested without revealing a lot, to the point that halfway through the book you may not know where the story is headed, but you are definitely heavily invested in the characters he has thoroughly developed by really getting you inside of their brains. Ultimately, the balance of humor and seriousness make Wellness an enjoyable, well-rounded story that I would gladly recommend to anyone with an open mind.

Title: Demon Copperhead
Author: Barbara Kingsolver
My Review:
Kingsolver’s citation of David Copperfield as THE inspiration for this novel seems unnecessary— let the book stand in its own; Demon Copperhead pretty much does.

The Good: Kingsolver’s passionate narrative causes the reader to feel “all the feels” of the protagonist, you are right there with him during his highest highs and his lowest lows.

The Bad: Unfortunately, this epic comes off a little "too epic", a little too self-aware, to the point that some of its moments are too cleanly packaged in a way that is obviously trying to live up to its own hype, and ends up falling a little flat because of it.

In the end, Kingsolver's tale has many beautiful, engrossing moments, but isn't able to weave a strong enough thread between the string of passionate episodes that are explored, ultimately leaving the reader scrambling to piece together a coherent thematic takeaway.

Title: Bluets
Author: Maggie Nelson
My Review:
3.5

The color blue has countless subtle variations, and Bluets captures all of its nuances through beautiful ruminations.

Nelson's thoughts are fragmented at times, and the transition between them can be a bit jarring, leaving little time for the reader to form coherent connections between them. However, that's okay, as Bluets is obviously more poetry than prose. Bluets' blue-hued cogitations may be better consumed in small doses, lest its reading become reminiscent of perusing an exhaustive catalogue of the color.

Despite any shortcomings of Bluets' continuity, the reader is sure to find valuable sapphire gems of insight among its pages. And so, stepping back to view her canvas as whole, Nelson has painted colorful visions with varying brushstrokes that yield an intricate tapestry of blues that is as deep as it is wide.

Title: The Past Is Red
Author: Catherynne M. Valente
My Review: The Past Is Red scores major points for its imaginative vision of a post-apocalyptic future.  Valente's novel is rife with lengthy descriptions of a world that isn't anchored in recognizable landmarks, and the humor of the narrator serves as much-needed comic relief to any disorientation the reader may feel.  Behind the tough exterior of both the protagonist and the world she lives in, there are treasures to be found, but the reader must show patience in wading through what feels a little like a short story that was made slightly too long in the attempt to be a novel.

Title: The Unbearable Lightness of Being
Author: Milan Kundera
My Review:
I guess it’s probably a sign the book isn’t that great when a dog ends up being your favorite character.

I’ll admit that parts this book went a bit over my head, but the parts I did understand weren’t that enjoyable.

There were a lot of moments where Kundera forgot the “show don’t tell” rule of writing. Yes, there are many cases where authors break this rule to great success, but I don’t consider this novel to be one of them.

Unfortunately, The Unbearable Lightness of Being ventures into “I’m 15 and this is deep” territory too many times to be good.

Thus, Patchett resorts to holding the  the reader’s attention through the many meandering thoughts of her characters, very few of which end up being all that memorable.

Title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
Author: Oscar Wilde
My Review: 3.5-- I'm between "liked" and "really liked". The Picture of Dorian Gray exceeded my expectations in some ways, but didn't quite live up to them in others. No doubt, Wilde's novel is full of quotable one-liners-- insightful bits of wisdom about life, youth, passion, art, and more. Ironically, a lot of sage advice comes from a despicable character who Wilde expertly crafts in such a way that the reader can only come away with a love/hate relationship. However, the reader's relationship with the story's protagonist is likely more one-sided-- his depth of character doesn't match his good looks. In the end, the reader can choose to be put off by Dorian's instability, or to view his malleability as a fascinating study of fickle human nature.

Title: Starry Messenger: Cosmic Perspectives on Civilization
Author: Neil deGrasse Tyson
My Review:
July 2022: ARC or Advanced Reader Copy, won in Goodreads giveaway -- thank you.

A quick, easy read-- Starry Messenger is a natural extension of the cosmic perspective ideas that Tyson touched on in Astrophysics for People in a Hurry. It's easy to get behind the spirit of the book-- taking a step back and looking at the big picture can give us the reset we need to view human civilization from a more unbiased perspective. Tyson excels when he focuses on exploring what our discoveries of the universe have revealed to us about life on earth, but at times it feels like the word "scientific" could be substituted for "cosmic" in the subtitle of the book. As always, Tyson's humor is a welcome constant and helps to make up for any lack of continuity in the "cosmic" theme. Once you get past the fact that Starry Messenger is loosely focused on the concept of what cosmic truths can teach us, you can really settle in and enjoy Tyson's quirky musings on the absurd and insightful aspects of humanity, and its hopeful striving for enlightenment and happiness.

Title: The Prospect of Immortality
Author: Robert C.W. Ettinger
My Review:
As one of the first important manifestos of the cryonics movement, Prospect of Immortality is a must-read for those curious about suspended animation. The use of the word "immortality" is frequently cited as a misnomer by many cryonicists, citing that the goal of cryonics is only to save humans in their present state from death, not to grant them eternal life. However, it is clear that Ettinger was of the strain of cryonicists that inextricably links successful reanimation to the technology that will also prolong life indefinitely.

The book's over-optimism is clear from the start--while it does not exactly use immortality as a synonym for being cryogenically preserved, it ties so many other hypothetical technological successes related to "immortality" to the successful revival of "freezees" that it leaves little room for doubt. Thus, immortality is not only an appropriate representation of the spirit of what Ettinger proposed, but it is also a clear sign of its excessive idealization.

In simple terms: Ettinger gets off track at times, but the valuable points he does make throughout and the core principles within still make Prospect of Immortality well worth the read.

Title: The Metamorphosis

Paradoxically, The Metamorphosis is both too drawn out and too simplistic. While I can appreciate Kafka’s message about human nature, he could have conveyed it in a story that was better executed and less infuriating.

My review of this book? "It is not important".

Title: The Tales of Beedle the Bard
Author: J.K. Rowling
My Review: 3.5 stars.  (I'd guess this would be more like a 4.5-5.0 for the Harry Potter-obsessed) Several of the stories were much more entertaining than the others, and Dumbledore's notes explaining each tale are a joy. I didn't like a couple of the stories because they didn't resonate with me or were too cliché.  However, "The Warlock's Hairy Heart" was pleasantly more dark and awesome than I expected any of this book's stories to be.  That one alone makes this worth checking out.  The other tale that was a highlight for me was "Babbitty Rabbitty and her Cackling Stump"-- lots of fun. Last but not least, the Tale of the Three Brothers is classic (if you are familiar with the HP books or films).

Title: A Man Called Ove
Author: Fredrik Backman
My Review: A Man Called Ove is a comedic novel about a crusty old man that immediately brings to mind Carl Fredricksen from Disney-Pixar's "Up".  Like "Up", this book can also tug at your heartstrings, as you follow Ove through all the stages of life and their accompanying emotions.  It's quite a fascinating look into what makes a person like Ove into the man he is, and how there is actually a lot more to him than meets the eye. Despite touching on some pretty dark subject matter, Fredrik Backman manages to put a positive spin on his book by putting its heavier themes into perspective. Overall, this was a fun read, and I think it's a novel I will be recommending to someone looking for a heartfelt book that is funny and insightful.

My Review: This book was quite the ride.  I admire the author’s ability to mingle deep and meaningful topics with the quirky humor of such a ridiculous story. It was mostly off-the-wall and ridiculous in a good way, and at times perhaps a bit overly sentimental. I found myself having more fun than not, so I consider it a better than average read. Ultimately, I think the author accomplished exactly what they set out to do, teach us about life through a varied cast of interesting characters that most of us can relate to.

Title: The Maidens
Author: Alex Michaelides
My Review: 2.5 out of 5 stars seems like the perfect rating to represent the half-baked feel of The Maidens.  This story had all the right ingredients, and so much potential, but in the end it just falls flat due to poor execution.  I read this practically back-to-back with The Silent Patient, and it’s clear that where that novel succeeded, this one has issues. The characters in The Maidens are less relatable and I think that that Michaelides relies too heavily on the plot to carry the reader through to the end of the book. But, unfortunately it was a struggle for me to finish this novel because many of the promising ideas contained within really missed the mark.

Title: 1Q84 (1Q84, #1-3)
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review: While it isn’t a book that I would recommend to everyone, there is a lot to love about 1Q84. The ethereal world Murakami created and the way its narratives intertwine is both fascinating and complex, with many whimsical touches.  With its rich imagery and character development, I will remember 1Q84 as something approximating a Hayao Miyazaki story for adults (for my  lack of a better comparison). Even with it being quite lengthy and at times repetitive, I was surprised that I found myself unable to abandon reading 1Q84. (I went in having accepted the possibility that I might give up reading due to its page count) Yes, the plot can be difficult to wrap your head around at a few points, but I would recommend 1Q84 to anyone craving a weird world and deep dives into the brains of a diverse set of characters. For me, it ended up being a good introduction to Murakami, and I very much look forward to exploring his other works.
